chapters.title: The Milk Shake Dilemma
chapters.hook: Vera passes the muffin case because the cup has to last the whole ride.
chapters.counterintuition: Teams spend months improving what a product is, but actually the reason it gets purchased lives entirely in the situation surrounding the buyer, not the object itself.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name one product being improved, then write the specific moment a buyer is in when they hire it, not their profile. If you cannot write that in 30 seconds, start there before the next feature discussion.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A product earns its place only after you name the progress it is hired to create in a specific circumstance, then identify every substitute competing to solve that same moment.

breakdown.fastRead: At 6:48 a.m., a commuter stands at a grab-and-go counter with muffins, bananas, and a thick sealed shake in front of her. The category label says dessert. The long drive says breakfast tool. She needs one hand free, something that will not crumble on her coat, and enough volume to outlast the boredom. The product is competing with every option that could get the same job done in the same moment. When teams ask what customers want changed, they often get useful surface data while the real question stays hidden: why was this hired in the first place? The job redraws the rival field. Start there.
breakdown.deepRead:
The useful question is not who buys this product. It is what job does the buyer need done right now, in this exact circumstance. A product description can be accurate and still explain almost nothing. A thick sealed drink is just a thick sealed drink until the long drive, the occupied hand, the dull highway, and the need to feel fed arrive together. Then it becomes a practical answer.

Picture a morning commuter covering forty-five minutes of interstate before a meeting. She is not making a health choice. She is managing a boring single-handed drive with one purchase. Thickness keeps the drink from disappearing in three sips. The sealed lid protects the gear shift. The slow pace of consuming it fills idle minutes at red lights. No flavor survey captures that bundle of constraints.

Now shift the moment. A parent buys the same product for a child after a youth sports session. The functional need is smaller. The social load is larger. The parent wants a manageable treat, a quick yes after a long game, and a purchase that closes the parking-lot stop without drama. Same product. Completely different job.

Once the job is visible, rivals no longer sit only inside the beverage category. The morning commuter is weighing a banana, a bagel, black coffee, or nothing at all. The parent after practice is weighing ice cream, a promise to stop later, or a quick speech about patience. Circumstance defines the field. Category labels do not.

Most product research breaks down here. Teams average the answers into roadmap items. The averaging smooths away the very pressure that explains the original hire. The right unit of analysis is the moment of struggle, not the profile of the buyer.
breakdown.fullRead:
For decades, the milkshake morning commute case has stayed useful because it catches a research mistake at the exact moment it feels sensible. A company wants to improve sales. Someone on the team designs a survey: what should be different, what would make this better. Sweeter, thicker, cheaper, more portable, bigger, smaller. Each answer sounds actionable. Each one arrives after the real causal question has already been bypassed: why did this buyer, in this circumstance, choose this option at all?

Jobs thinking changes the unit of analysis entirely. A buyer standing at a kiosk on her morning commute is not a demographic segment. She is a person with a 45-minute drive, an occupied left hand, a meeting she needs to arrive at awake, and a need for something that stays clean and lasts the whole drive. Those constraints are the job. They exist before she opens the cooler door. When teams see that bundle clearly, they can evaluate every feature, price, and format change against it. Without it, improvements become guesses dressed up as data.

Morning commuters hired the thick sealed shake because it was slow to consume, portable enough to manage one-handed, and filling enough to handle a long drive. It beat a banana because the banana was gone in ninety seconds and left a sticky hand. It beat a muffin because crumbs land on dark coats. It beat black coffee because caffeine without calories does not address the hunger. These are the architectural reasons the product won that morning, and none of them would show up in a satisfaction survey asking about sweetness or price.

Shift the circumstance and the job changes entirely. A parent buying the same product for a child after a youth sports session is not managing a drive. The child is tired and wants recognition more than nutrition. The parent wants a clean yes, a visible reward after a hard game, and a purchase that does not extend the parking-lot stop into a negotiation over candy. The cup can still spill in a back seat, a constraint absent from the highway. Same product name on the receipt. Different job. Different competitor set. Different standard for success.

This is why the method has to separate occasions before it permits any averaging. When a team blends morning commuters and post-game parents into a single user persona, they smooth away the pressures that made each hire happen. The resulting roadmap optimizes for a buyer who never faced either circumstance sharply.

The competitive field also changes when you name the job. A morning shake competes with a banana, a bagel, a protein bar, black coffee, or skipped breakfast entirely. A parent-child treat competes with ice cream, a vending machine snack, a promised stop later, or a patient lecture. None of those substitutes sits inside the beverage category. But they all get hired for the same jobs on the right morning or afternoon.

Product features still matter. Thickness, cup shape, lid design, price, and taste are all load-bearing. The point is sequence. Features earn their place after the team understands the job they must serve. Without that anchor, every improvement is a guess. With it, the team can ask precisely: does this change help the specific progress that made the product worth hiring in the first place? That question turns product work from preference chasing into judgment. The circumstance is the specification. The job is the standard.

examples.title: Vera watches the wrong survey at the grab-and-go kiosk

planSpec.audience: brand product manager shadowing a commuter observation session
planSpec.stakes: her survey asks the wrong question while the real job plays out in front of her
planSpec.requiredBeat: Vera watches a commuter bypass the healthier option and take the thick sealed shake, realizing the commuter is managing a 45-minute ride one-handed, not making a health decision

examples.scenario: The kiosk smells of hot coffee and warm pastry at 7:48 a.m. Vera stands two steps back with her clipboard, watching a commuter reach past the granola cups and banana display to pull a thick sealed shake from the cooler. The survey in Vera's hand asks about flavor, portion, and price. The commuter is not weighing any of those. She is about to board a train with one free hand and forty-five minutes of nothing to do, and the sealed cup is the only option that will last the whole ride without a mess.
examples.whatToDo: Pause the survey. Write down the commuter's visible constraints: one occupied hand, a long ride, a need for volume that outlasts the trip. Only after naming those can you design a question worth asking.
examples.whyItMatters: When the circumstance drives the hire, feature questions arrive too late. Vera's clipboard captures preferences; the kiosk behavior captures the job. The two are not the same data.

examples.title: Laurent traces the return spike to the wrong improvement

planSpec.audience: brand manager reviewing a return spike after adding features power users requested
planSpec.stakes: new features pleased one job while breaking another
planSpec.requiredBeat: Laurent takes a return call from a physical therapy patient who says the new guide assumes I already know what I am doing, revealing the recovery job versus the performance job

examples.scenario: Laurent pulls the return data at 2:15 p.m., four weeks after launching the upgraded resistance band set with the detailed progression guide power users had requested. The chart shows a 34-percent spike in the 40-to-60 age bracket. He calls a returner. "The new guide assumes I already know what I am doing," the woman says. "My therapist recommended this after my hip replacement. I need someone to tell me where to start." Laurent is weighing whether to split the SKU or back out the guide.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the two jobs before changing the product again. The performance job and the recovery job share a price point but require different onboarding, different language, and different proof of success.
examples.whyItMatters: Power-user feedback is valid data for one job. It is wrong data for a different job riding the same SKU. Laurent's upgrade served the wrong customer by asking only the loudest one.

examples.title: Sofía hears the real reason the cocoa kit sells at the lodge

planSpec.domain: mountain lodge gift shop selling hot cocoa kits
planSpec.audience: lodge retail manager comparing lodge sales to grocery store performance
planSpec.stakes: same product moves at the lodge and sits at the grocery store two valleys down
planSpec.requiredBeat: a customer says I am not even a cocoa person while buying it, and Sofía realizes the job is 20 quiet indoor minutes for two kids while adults rest, a job the lodge circumstance creates entirely

examples.scenario: Sofía watches a woman in ski pants set the foil cocoa kit on the counter. "I am not even a cocoa person," the woman says, while two kids chase each other around the display rack. Outside, sleet hits the windows. "But they need something to do for twenty minutes while we dry out." Sofía rings it up and watches the family head toward the fireplace. The same kit sits unsold at a grocery store two valleys down. Sofía faces a choice: lower the grocery price, or understand why the lodge sells a product the buyer does not prefer.
examples.whatToDo: Name the lodge circumstance as the job creator. Wet weather, tired adults, two restless children, and twenty minutes indoors combine to make the kit hireable. The grocery store context provides none of those forces.
examples.whyItMatters: The product did not change between the lodge shelf and the valley shelf. The circumstance did. Sofía is not selling cocoa at the lodge; she is selling a twenty-minute solution to a specific indoor problem.

examples.title: You are Marco at the print center at 11:30 p.m.

planSpec.audience: print center manager and through second-person the reader facing the queue decision
planSpec.stakes: the buyer at 11:30pm is not choosing paper quality
planSpec.requiredBeat: at 11:30pm with a 7am thesis deadline, the buyer is hiring speed and certainty to eliminate the anxiety of a failed reprint at 3am

examples.scenario: You are Marco, standing at the print center counter at 11:30 p.m. A student with a thesis folder needs to decide between the standard queue (90 minutes, cheaper) and the priority lane (12 minutes, twice the price). Her deadline is 7 a.m. She is not comparing paper stock or binding quality. She is weighing the risk of a 3 a.m. failed print job against a price premium now. The job is not printing. The job is certainty that the document exists, finished and in her hand, before anxiety brings her back out of bed.
examples.whatToDo: Price the priority lane against anxiety elimination, not against paper cost. If the student is hiring certainty, the competitor is not a cheaper queue, it is the fear of a 3 a.m. crisis.
examples.whyItMatters: Marco's queue options look identical on a feature comparison. The circumstance makes them completely different hires. The job is visible only after you name what the buyer needs to stop worrying about.

examples.title: At 9:03 a.m., Astrid's prediction is wrong by a factor of three

planSpec.audience: HR manager reviewing benefit take-up rates
planSpec.stakes: Astrid predicted yoga leads but meal delivery credits led 3 to 1
planSpec.requiredBeat: at 9:03am Astrid's prediction that yoga leads is wrong; meal delivery credits led 3 to 1, and three users say it kept the household running during crunch weeks, revealing the job as operational stability, not nutrition

examples.scenario: At 9:03 a.m., Astrid opens the Q1 enrollment dashboard and reads her own prediction sticky note: yoga leads, nutrition second. Meal delivery credits led 3 to 1. She pulls three exit interviews. Each says the same thing: during crunch weeks, dinner was the first thing that fell apart and the credit kept the household running. Astrid needs to decide whether to add more yoga options for next year or reframe the entire benefit narrative.
examples.whatToDo: Read the enrollment data against household circumstance, not wellness category. The job employees hired was operational stability during high-pressure work cycles, not nutrition improvement.
examples.whyItMatters: Astrid was measuring by product category. The employees were hiring by household survival. The gap between those two framings explains the entire prediction error.

examples.title: Bruno misreads a 3 to 1 scent ratio as preference

planSpec.audience: market vendor who has misread a 3 to 1 lavender-to-citrus ratio as scent preference
planSpec.stakes: over-ordering lavender based on wrong interpretation of the ratio
planSpec.requiredBeat: a buyer picks up lavender and says this is what my mom's bathroom smelled like on Sunday mornings, revealing the product is hired to restore an emotional state, not for cleansing quality

examples.scenario: Bruno restacks the lavender bars at the corner of the market table, proud of the 3-to-1 sales ratio over citrus. A woman in her fifties picks up a bar, presses it to her wrist, and says quietly: "This is what my mom's bathroom smelled like on Sunday mornings." She buys four. Bruno has to decide whether to double the lavender order before next weekend, based on what looks like a clear preference signal, except the signal is not about scent preference at all.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the emotional job from the product attribute. The lavender bar is being hired to restore a specific memory and feeling, not because buyers prefer lavender as a cleansing ingredient. That job may not scale with more inventory.
examples.whyItMatters: Bruno's ratio looks like demand data. It is actually emotional hire data. Ordering more lavender addresses the supply side of the wrong question; understanding the restoration job addresses the right one.

questions.prompt: A commuter bypasses a healthier option and grabs a thick sealed shake at 7:48 a.m. A product team is reviewing this observation. Which question best reveals the job being hired?
choices: What flavor profile would this buyer prefer if we offered three new varieties?
What constraints in this commuter's morning make a thick sealed drink the clearest solution?
Which demographic segment does this buyer belong to and what are their average preferences?
questions.explanation: The commuter's constraints, one free hand, a long ride, a need for lasting volume, are the job specification. Flavor and demographic data arrive only after that causal question is answered.

questions.prompt: A product team adds features that power users requested. Returns spike from a different segment. Applying the circumstance lens, what should the team investigate first?
choices: Whether the two buyer groups are hiring the product for different jobs that now conflict on the same SKU.
Whether the price is positioned correctly for the returning segment.
Whether the marketing message is reaching the right demographic channels.
questions.explanation: When an improvement pleases one group and alienates another, two distinct jobs likely share one SKU. Investigating price or marketing first skips the more fundamental question about competing jobs.

questions.prompt: A hot cocoa kit sells well at a mountain lodge during winter but sits unsold at a grocery store two valleys away. Same product, same price. Which explanation fits the circumstance lens?
choices: The lodge may simply attract more families with young children, while the grocery draws routine pantry shoppers, so audience mix could explain the sales pattern.
The lodge may place the kit beside fireside activities, while the grocery buries it in a cocoa aisle, so display context could be the missing variable.
The lodge environment creates a job, wet weather plus restless children plus indoor time, that the grocery store context does not provide.
questions.explanation: The circumstance at the lodge produces the hiring moment: adults needing quiet, children needing activity, weather forcing everyone indoors. The product did not change; the surrounding job did.

questions.prompt: At 11:30 p.m. before a 7 a.m. thesis deadline, a student chooses a 12-minute priority print lane over a 90-minute cheaper queue. Using the jobs lens, what is the real substitute the student is comparing?
choices: Other print shops with similar overnight services in the area.
The standard queue, which has identical output quality at a lower price.
The anxiety of a 3 a.m. failed print attempt versus the certainty of holding the document now.
questions.explanation: Late at night before a high-stakes deadline, the student is hiring certainty to eliminate a future anxiety, not comparing print queues by cost. That reframes both the product and its real competitor.

questions.prompt: An HR manager predicted yoga would lead benefit enrollment. Meal delivery credits led 3 to 1. Exit interviews say the credit kept households running during crunch weeks. What does the circumstance lens reveal?
choices: Employees hired the meal credit to maintain household operations under work pressure, a job the wellness category framing missed entirely.
Employees generally prefer practical benefits over wellness benefits regardless of circumstance.
The benefit communication for yoga was inadequate and should be improved before drawing conclusions.
questions.explanation: The enrollment data makes sense only after naming the circumstance: high-pressure work weeks where dinner preparation collapses. That operational stability job has nothing to do with nutrition category preferences.

questions.prompt: A vendor sells lavender soap at a 3-to-1 ratio over citrus. A buyer says the scent restores a childhood memory of her mother's bathroom. Applying the jobs lens, what should the vendor examine before doubling the lavender order?
choices: Whether the lavender fragrance formulation can be strengthened to appeal to more buyers.
Whether the 3-to-1 ratio reflects emotional hire patterns that may not scale with added inventory.
Whether citrus is simply a weaker scent category in the regional market.
questions.explanation: A memory-restoration job is tied to a specific emotional circumstance, not a general scent preference. Treating the ratio as preference data rather than emotional occasion data leads to the wrong stocking decision.

questions.prompt: A team realizes morning commuters and post-game parents both buy the same beverage. They plan to average the two groups into one persona. What does the circumstance lens say they will lose?
choices: The brand consistency that comes from serving a single clear identity across contexts.
The distinct pressures, substitutes, and success criteria that explain why each group hired the product.
The ability to run a single focused advertising campaign that resonates with both groups.
questions.explanation: Averaging occasions removes the specific constraints behind each hire. The commuter job and the parent-child treat job have different competitors, different failure modes, and different design requirements that disappear in the average.

questions.prompt: A team improves a product based on power-user feedback. Returns spike from a recovery-patient segment. Which evaluation best describes what went wrong?
choices: The team gathered valid data for one job and applied it as if it explained a different job sharing the same SKU.
The team failed to communicate the new features clearly to the recovery-patient segment.
The recovery-patient segment has lower product literacy and needs better onboarding materials.
questions.explanation: Power-user feedback is accurate for the performance job. It is the wrong data for the recovery job. The error was treating feedback from one hiring occasion as guidance for a different one that happened to share a product name.

questions.prompt: A team asks survey respondents: what would you change about this product? They get answers about flavor, size, and price. Which limitation does the circumstance lens expose in this research design?
choices: Survey responses are inherently unreliable and should be replaced with ethnographic observation.
The sample size is too small to produce statistically significant feature rankings.
The survey gathers preference data after the causal question, why was this hired at all, has already been skipped.
questions.explanation: Preference surveys assume the team already understands why the product gets hired. They arrive after the real question. Starting with the moment of struggle reveals what the product must actually accomplish before any feature is worth testing.

reviewCards.front: What question does the circumstance lens replace 'who is our customer?' with?
reviewCards.back: What job does this buyer need done right now, in this specific situation? The buyer's profile is secondary. The moment of struggle is primary.

reviewCards.front: A product sells in one location and sits unsold in another. Same price, same shelf placement. What should you examine first?
reviewCards.back: Examine the surrounding circumstance. The job may exist in one location and be absent in the other. The product did not change; the hiring moment did.

reviewCards.front: Two customer groups buy the same product. The team averages them into one persona. What is lost?
reviewCards.back: The distinct pressures, substitute sets, and success criteria for each hiring occasion. Averaging smooths away the exact forces that explain each purchase.

reviewCards.front: Power-user feedback drives a product update. A different segment returns the product in large numbers. What does this pattern suggest?
reviewCards.back: Two jobs may share one SKU. Feedback from one hiring occasion was applied to a different one. Separate the jobs before the next product decision.

reviewCards.front: A team runs a feature preference survey. Where does the circumstance lens say the analysis needs to start?
reviewCards.back: One step earlier: the moment of struggle that created the hire. Preference data answers the wrong question if the team has not yet explained why the product got hired at all.

implementationPlan.title: Mapping the Buyer's Hiring Moment
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Before any product decision, write the buyer's exact moment: time, place, constraint, and what old approach was being replaced. Check that every proposed change improves that specific moment, not a hypothetical average user.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a feature debate starts, then write the buyer's circumstance at the top of the whiteboard and force every candidate feature to answer which constraint it removes from that moment.
If a wellness product or routine is not sticking, then name the exact moment it needs to work in, not the general habit goal, and judge it against that live constraint.
If a purchase feels oddly satisfying or oddly disappointing, then pause and write what circumstance made you hire it and whether the product actually served that moment.
If someone keeps rejecting your suggestions, then ask what specific situation they are in right now and what would count as progress before offering another option.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, catch yourself making one hiring decision, anything from a food choice to a tool selection. Write the clock time, the constraint that triggered it, and one sentence naming what progress you were trying to make. Check whether what you hired actually served that moment.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, watch someone make a purchase or choice without asking them about it. Afterward, reconstruct the circumstance: what was the push away from the old option, what made the hired choice feel like the answer, and what would have served that moment better.

memorableLines.text: Circumstance defines the field. Category labels do not.
memorableLines.why: It reframes competition in one sentence, replacing product-category thinking with situation-based thinking.

memorableLines.text: Features earn their place after the team understands the job they must serve.
memorableLines.why: It gives the correct sequence for product work: job first, features second.

memorableLines.text: The circumstance is the specification. The job is the standard.
memorableLines.why: It closes the argument by naming what replaces preference data as the design anchor.

chapters.title: Progress, Not Products
chapters.hook: Claire's groom-quality scores are green and her churn is red, and the gap is a dog hiding under a bed.
chapters.counterintuition: Progress is not a functional upgrade. It is a specific movement from a strained state to a better one, and the dimensions a buyer cares about most are often the ones teams never thought to measure.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name the last product your team shipped. Write three lines: the practical result it creates, how the buyer appears to others, and how they feel about themselves. If line three is blank, you are missing part of the job.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before any design decision, name the full movement the buyer wants to make: the practical change, the status shift, and the emotional change when it works.

breakdown.fastRead: Claire's dog grooming subscription has perfect quality scores and rising churn. The exit interviews say the same thing: every Friday he hid under the bed. The groom quality was not the job. The job was that the dog's experience, and the owner's guilt about it, had to be bearable. That is the distinction between a product and progress. Progress names a movement from a strained state to a better one, and that movement has functional, social, and emotional layers. When a team tracks only the functional layer, it can build an expertly run service that still fails the hire entirely. The full job includes how the buyer feels about themselves when it works.
breakdown.deepRead:
Progress is more precise than satisfaction. It names a movement from a current circumstance toward a better state. The current state has friction, risk, delay, or discomfort. The better state has a shape the buyer can recognize when it arrives. A buyer may want the form filed, the dog calm, the invoice paid, or the room less humiliating. But behind each of those functional outcomes is usually a social story and an emotional one.

At 10:55 in the morning, in a yoga studio office, Étienne faces a member who is pausing her membership. She has been coming for three years. She says the classes are fine. Then she adds: "It is the one hour where I am not managing anyone's feelings." The functional product was adequate. But she hired the studio for social relief, one hour of not being the caregiver, and the emotional change that comes with that. If Étienne treats her pause as a pricing negotiation, he misses the job entirely.

This is why social and emotional forces are part of the work, not decorations around it. A tool that solves the task while making the buyer feel exposed can still lose. A service that delivers less technical capability but lets the buyer feel capable or relieved can win. The discipline is keeping progress tied to a specific circumstance. If the framing expands into happiness or fulfillment without a concrete before-and-after, it stops guiding any decision. Name the before state, name the better state, and hold both close enough to test.
breakdown.fullRead:
A product is a thing. Progress is a change. That difference sounds abstract until a team tries to explain why a customer chose one answer over another, stayed for three years and then left, or returned the upgraded version of something they loved.

The movement a buyer wants usually has three layers operating at the same time. Functional progress is the visible layer: the dog is calm, the document is filed, the car starts, the dinner is on the table. Social progress is about how the buyer appears to or is positioned among other people: the parent looks responsible, the new employee does not seem lost, the patient does not feel like a burden. Emotional progress is about the internal state that shifts when the answer works: the buyer feels calmer, less exposed, less guilty, more ready, or simply less stuck.

Those layers rarely separate cleanly in a live circumstance. Giulia manages a bookshop with a café. She expanded the café because traffic was up. Transaction size has dropped. When she watches remote workers arrive at nine in the morning and leave at noon, buying two lattes and one book, she realizes they are not buying coffee and literature. They are hiring a third place: a functional workspace, a social signal that they are working-but-not-at-home, and an emotional permission to sit without guilt for three hours. The café expansion did not fail because of pricing. It created a second job that now competes with the first one for the same physical space.

Good product work does not rank those layers too early. It listens for how they combine in the specific circumstance. Devon manages a driving range. Survey data says members want to improve power. Observation shows Friday evening pairs arriving together, staying two hours, hitting the same bucket at a relaxed pace. The job is not power improvement. It is low-stakes outdoor social activity with a physical prop. If Devon invests in premium bays designed for serious training, he optimizes for the stated preference while removing the relaxed environment that makes the social job possible.

The useful test is concreteness. A claim that buyers want confidence is too broad until the team can point to the situation where confidence is absent and describe what would be different if it were present. Confidence before a presentation, after a medical diagnosis, during a first gym session, or in front of a teenager's homework are not the same job. Each has different substitutes, different signals of success, and different design requirements.

This also explains why buyers seem inconsistent. The same person chooses a premium option in one moment and the cheapest option in another. The person did not change. The progress target changed. When a team can see the full three-layer movement clearly, and hold it to a specific before-and-after in a real circumstance, product decisions become less like preference guessing and more like helping a buyer cross a specific gap they have already identified. That gap is the specification. Functional, social, and emotional progress together are the standard.

examples.title: At 9:11 a.m., Claire's quality data is green and her churn dashboard is red

planSpec.stakes: quality scores are high but churn is rising and the exit data points somewhere unexpected
planSpec.requiredBeat: at 9:11am Claire's groom-quality data is green but churn is red; exit interviews say every Friday he hid under the bed, revealing that the emotional progress job, the dog's experience plus the owner's guilt, drove the cancellation

examples.scenario: At 9:11 a.m., Claire opens the monthly dashboard with her prediction sticky note still visible: quality score up, churn stable. Quality is up. Churn is up too. She pulls the exit interview transcripts and reads the same line in different forms: every Friday he hid under the bed, he shook when I picked up his leash, I felt terrible the whole day. The grooms were excellent by every measure the team tracked. She must decide whether to rebuild the service around dog comfort or defend the quality scores.
examples.whatToDo: Add the emotional progress layer to the cancellation review. Track whether the dog's experience of the service, and the owner's feeling about it, meets the same standard as technical groom quality.
examples.whyItMatters: A technically excellent service can fail the emotional dimension of the job entirely. Claire's metrics captured the product. They missed the progress the owner was actually trying to make.

examples.title: Étienne hears the hour that has nothing to do with yoga

planSpec.audience: studio co-owner in pause negotiation with a long-term member
planSpec.stakes: a three-year member is pausing and the reason is not the classes
planSpec.requiredBeat: the member says it is the one hour where I am not managing anyone's feelings, revealing that the functional product was hired for a social progress job: relief from a caregiving role

examples.scenario: "The classes are fine," Valentina says, sitting across from Étienne at 10:55 a.m. with her membership card on the table. "I am just burned out." Étienne is about to offer a discounted pause rate when she adds: "It is the one hour where I am not managing anyone's feelings. Not my kids, not my team, not my mother." Étienne sets the pricing sheet aside. The studio is one of the only hours in Valentina's week that belongs entirely to her, and she needs him to understand that before money enters the room.
examples.whatToDo: Name the social progress job before negotiating on price. Valentina hired the membership for relief from a caregiving role. A discount does not address that job; a different framing of what the hour is for might.
examples.whyItMatters: Three years of attendance built around a social progress job will not be retained by a product improvement. Étienne needs to understand the job before he can offer anything relevant.

examples.title: Giulia traces traffic up and transaction size down to a second job

planSpec.audience: bookshop manager reviewing traffic-up but transaction-size-down after café expansion
planSpec.stakes: the café expansion changed who is hiring the space and for what
planSpec.requiredBeat: remote workers stay 3 hours, buy 2 lattes and 1 book as a cover charge; the café is hired as a third place with a functional workspace job, a social not-home-not-office job, and an emotional acceptable-loitering job; two distinct jobs now compete for the same space

examples.scenario: Giulia reviews the monthly P&L at 4:30 p.m. on a Tuesday. Foot traffic is up 28 percent since the café expansion. Average transaction is down 19 percent. She walks the floor and counts: fourteen people with laptops, three with books, two browsing. A remote worker at table seven has been there since 9 a.m., bought two lattes and one paperback. Giulia needs to decide before next quarter whether the café created a new job for a new buyer, or broke the original job for the old one.
examples.whatToDo: Name both jobs explicitly before making any floor or pricing change. The third-place job and the browse-and-buy job may be incompatible in the same physical space at the same time.
examples.whyItMatters: The café expansion succeeded at creating a new hiring occasion. It also introduced a conflict between two jobs competing for the same resource: space, quiet, and atmosphere. Giulia cannot optimize for both without first naming each.

examples.title: You are Thomas, and you need to name the job before choosing the venue

planSpec.audience: operations manager choosing between hotel conference center and farmhouse through second-person
planSpec.stakes: the real progress job is forcing remote workers to be genuinely present together without the escape hatch of normal work mode
planSpec.requiredBeat: the real progress job is forcing remote workers to be genuinely present together without the escape hatch of normal work mode; the farmhouse wins because it removes the wifi distraction; Thomas needs to name the job before choosing

examples.scenario: You are Thomas. The hotel has fast wifi, breakout rooms, and a catering team. The farmhouse forty minutes outside has slow internet, one long dining table, and nowhere to take a side call. Your budget covers either. Reservations close Friday and you are about to choose. The real progress job for this offsite is not completing the agenda. It is making twelve remote colleagues spend two days genuinely present together, without the escape hatch of a Slack channel pulling someone into a corner. You must decide which space gives that a real chance.
examples.whatToDo: Name the job before evaluating the venue features. If the job is genuine presence, the farmhouse's friction is a feature, not a flaw. Choose against the job, not against the amenities checklist.
examples.whyItMatters: Thomas cannot make a good venue decision by comparing room sizes and catering menus. The right choice depends entirely on which environment creates the conditions for the progress he is actually trying to make.

examples.title: Maja discovers the morning voice job behind the pledge number

planSpec.audience: pledge drive coordinator with 40 percent below-target conversion
planSpec.stakes: the appeal is built around journalism, but the job is something different
planSpec.requiredBeat: donors are not preserving journalism; they are keeping one familiar voice on during morning commutes; functional job is companionship, emotional job is managing start-of-day anxiety; journalism is the category, not the job

examples.scenario: Maja stands at the pledge drive whiteboard at 8:40 a.m. with conversion rates 40 percent below last year's goal. The campaign says: support local journalism. Three listener interviews are pinned to the board. All three say the same thing in different ways: it is what I put on when I am getting ready, it is just on in the background, it is the voice I know. None of them mention journalism. Maja must decide whether to rewrite the appeal around a different story before the drive closes on Friday.
examples.whatToDo: Build the appeal around companionship during the morning transition, not the journalism category. Test whether donors respond to losing the familiar voice rather than losing investigative reporting.
examples.whyItMatters: Journalism is what the station produces. Manageable morning anxiety is what the listeners are hiring the station to reduce. Those are not the same job, and they require a completely different appeal.

examples.title: Devon needs to name the social job before picking the investment

planSpec.audience: sports facility manager deciding between premium bays and short-game area
planSpec.stakes: survey says power improvement; observation says something different
planSpec.requiredBeat: survey says power improvement; observation shows Friday evening pairs arriving together, staying 2 hours; the job is low-stakes outdoor social activity with a physical prop; Devon needs to name the social progress job before choosing the investment

examples.scenario: Devon is weighing two capital requests: automated launch monitors for four premium bays at forty thousand, or a short-game area with casual seating at twenty-two thousand. The member survey says power improvement is the top priority. He walks the range Friday evening and sees something the survey missed: pairs sharing a bucket, staying ninety minutes, rarely checking swing data. He needs to decide whether the survey or the observation answers the right question about what members actually hire the range to do.
examples.whatToDo: Name the social progress job the Friday observation reveals before presenting the request. If members hire the range for low-stakes outdoor social time, the short-game area may serve that job better than launch monitors.
examples.whyItMatters: Survey answers reflect stated preferences in the abstract. Observed behavior reflects the job in action. Devon needs to know which one he is designing for before spending forty thousand dollars.

questions.prompt: A dog grooming subscription has perfect quality scores but rising churn. Exit interviews mention the dog hiding under the bed before each appointment. Which progress dimension did the team fail to track?
choices: The functional dimension: whether the groom was completed on time and to specification.
The emotional dimension: whether the owner felt good about the dog's experience each week.
The social dimension: whether the dog's appearance improved the owner's reputation among neighbors.
questions.explanation: Quality scores track the functional output. The owner's guilt about the dog's visible distress belongs to the emotional progress layer, and that layer was driving cancellation regardless of technical quality.

questions.prompt: A yoga studio member says she attends because it is the one hour where she is not managing anyone's feelings. Which progress dimension should the studio owner address to understand the retention job?
choices: Social: the relief from caregiving obligations that the studio hour provides.
Functional: whether the class format matches her fitness goals and skill level.
Emotional: whether the music and studio temperature create a relaxing physical atmosphere.
questions.explanation: The member named relief from managing other people's needs, which is a social progress job. She is not hiring yoga instruction; she is hiring a structured hour that belongs entirely to her. A discount or class upgrade does not address that job.

questions.prompt: A bookshop expands with a café. Traffic rises but average transaction size falls. Remote workers stay three hours and buy one book as what feels like a cover charge. What does the progress lens reveal?
choices: The café pricing is too low relative to competitor coffee shops in the neighborhood.
The inventory selection is insufficiently curated for the type of customer the café is attracting.
Two distinct jobs, a third-place workspace job and a bookshop browsing job, are now competing for the same physical space.
questions.explanation: Remote workers are hiring the space for a third-place job: functional workspace, social legitimacy for lingering, and emotional permission to not be at home or in a formal office. That job conflicts with the browse-and-buy job for the same resource.

questions.prompt: An operations manager is choosing a company offsite venue. The real goal is getting remote workers genuinely present with each other without the normal work-mode escape hatch. Applying the progress lens, which venue feature matters most?
choices: Environmental conditions that remove the usual escape routes and make genuine presence easier.
Fast wifi and professional breakout rooms that allow parallel work streams during the offsite.
A catering team that handles all logistics so the manager can focus on the agenda.
questions.explanation: When the progress job is genuine presence, friction is a feature. A venue that removes normal-work-mode escape options directly serves the job. Amenities that make it easier to retreat into regular work patterns work against it.

questions.prompt: A radio pledge drive built around 'support local journalism' is 40 percent below its conversion target. Listener interviews say they tune in for a familiar voice during morning routines. Which diagnosis fits the progress lens?
choices: The journalism framing is too highbrow for the station's listener demographic.
The appeal targets the product category, not the emotional job listeners are actually hiring the station to do.
The pledge drive is too early in the season and should be moved to a higher-engagement time of year.
questions.explanation: Listeners are hiring the station to manage morning-routine anxiety through a familiar companionship cue, not to fund investigative reporting. The journalism frame describes what the station produces, not the progress listeners are trying to make.

questions.prompt: A driving range survey says members want power improvement. Friday evening observation shows pairs staying 90 minutes sharing a bucket at a relaxed pace. Which source of evidence is more useful for the investment decision?
choices: The survey, because it directly captures stated member priorities and preferences.
Both equally, combined into a weighted average to determine the most popular feature.
The observation, because it shows what job members are actually hiring the range to do on a specific occasion.
questions.explanation: Survey data reflects abstract stated preferences. Observed behavior reflects the live job in a specific circumstance. The Friday evening pattern reveals a social progress job that a power-improvement investment would fail to serve.

questions.prompt: A buyer chooses a premium option in one situation and the cheapest option in another. A product team labels this inconsistent behavior. What does the progress lens suggest instead?
choices: The buyer's progress target changed between situations, making different options the right hire for each moment.
The buyer has unstable preferences and needs clearer messaging to form consistent product loyalty.
The premium positioning is not clear enough, and the buyer defaults to price when uncertain.
questions.explanation: Buyers are not inconsistent; their progress targets shift by circumstance. The same person hires different options because the functional, social, or emotional job they need done differs in each situation.

questions.prompt: A team wants to improve user confidence. Which version of this progress goal is specific enough to guide a design decision?
choices: Users should feel more confident overall after using the product for 30 days.
Confidence should be a key brand value communicated through the product's visual design and copy.
A first-time user completing their initial setup should feel capable enough to use the product without asking for help.
questions.explanation: Progress goals require a concrete before state, a specific circumstance, and a recognizable better state. Option C names the circumstance, the starting condition, and the target state precisely enough to test and observe.

questions.prompt: A team identifies the functional progress their product creates but leaves the social and emotional dimensions blank. What risk does this introduce?
choices: The team will over-invest in emotional design at the expense of core functional reliability.
The product roadmap will expand too broadly and lose focus on the primary use case.
The product may satisfy the practical task while failing the dimensions of the job that drive retention and recommendation.
questions.explanation: A service can execute the functional task correctly and still fail the hire if the social or emotional layer drives the decision to stay or leave. Claire's grooming subscription is the exact example: perfect functional output, failed emotional job.

reviewCards.front: What are the three layers of progress a buyer may be making at the same time?
reviewCards.back: Functional progress: a practical change in their situation. Social progress: a shift in how they appear to or relate to others. Emotional progress: a change in how they feel about themselves.

reviewCards.front: A product has perfect quality scores and rising churn. What should you examine that the quality metrics cannot show?
reviewCards.back: Examine the social and emotional dimensions of the job. Technical quality tracks the functional output. If the buyer's social or emotional progress is not being served, excellent functional scores will not prevent cancellation.

reviewCards.front: A buyer stays three years and then leaves. Nothing about the product changed. Where does the progress lens direct your investigation?
reviewCards.back: Investigate whether the buyer's circumstance changed such that the job the product was hired to do no longer needs doing, or a different job became primary. Retention loss does not always mean product failure.

reviewCards.front: A team writes 'users want confidence' as a progress goal. What is missing?
reviewCards.back: A concrete before state, a specific circumstance, and a recognizable better state. Confidence in what situation, compared to what starting point, with what observable signal that the progress happened?

reviewCards.front: Survey data says one thing; field observation says another. Which one does the progress lens treat as more reliable?
reviewCards.back: Observation of behavior in a specific circumstance is more reliable than stated preferences in the abstract. Surveys capture what people believe they want; observation captures what job they are actually hiring a product to do.

implementationPlan.title: Writing a Three-Layer Progress Statement
implementationPlan.coreSkill: For any product or service, write a complete three-layer progress statement: the functional movement, the social change, and the emotional shift the buyer experiences when the job is done well. Hold all three against the circumstance before making any design or investment decision.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a product review focuses only on functional metrics, then ask the team to fill in the social and emotional columns before the review closes. If either is blank, pause the decision.
If a wellness tool or habit is not sticking, then write what functional, social, and emotional progress it was supposed to create. Check whether the tool serves all three in the actual moment of use.

If you keep returning to a particular product, place, or routine, then name what three-layer progress it delivers. That clarity helps you find or build better substitutes when the original is unavailable.

If someone's feedback about a product or service surprises you, then ask what state they were in before they used it and what state they expected to be in after. The gap names the progress they were hiring it to make.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, pick one thing you use regularly and write three sentences: what functional problem it solves, how it affects how you appear or relate to others, and how it changes how you feel about yourself. If any sentence is vague, make it concrete before you stop.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, ask someone why they stopped using something they used to rely on. Do not accept the first answer. Probe for the social and emotional layers beneath the functional explanation. The real job is usually in the second or third answer.

memorableLines.text: A product is a thing. Progress is a change.
memorableLines.why: It states the core distinction in six words, making it easy to retrieve and hard to misremember.

memorableLines.text: The full job includes how the buyer feels about themselves when it works.
memorableLines.why: It extends the job definition beyond functional output and names the emotional layer as a design requirement, not an afterthought.

memorableLines.text: That gap is the specification. Functional, social, and emotional progress together are the standard.
memorableLines.why: It closes the chapter's argument by naming all three layers as the measurement standard, replacing a purely functional design target.

chapters.title: Jobs in the Wild
chapters.hook: Emily learns the valet lot lost to a photo of level 3B taken at midnight.
chapters.counterintuition: The jobs lens is claimed to travel across any domain, but it only proves itself when you take it somewhere no case study has visited yet and let observable evidence decide.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick a product outside your work. Write: the circumstance that triggers the hire, the progress you seek, and the alternatives you considered. If the job differs from the stated purpose, you have proved portability.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Carry the three-part diagnostic into a domain you have never mapped before. If the evidence still holds, you have proved portability rather than assumed it.

breakdown.fastRead: Emily interviews frequent flyers about valet parking and expects the answer to be about price or ease. What she hears is about certainty. A traveler who lands at midnight after a delay needs to know exactly which level the car is on before the doors open. A self-park space circled in a photo on a phone does that job. Valet cannot. The three-part method travels to an airport garage and finds something nobody predicted from the category label. That is portability proved, not assumed.
breakdown.deepRead:
A lens that only works on famous examples is a story, not a method. The discipline test comes when you carry it into a domain nobody has written up, apply the three questions plainly, and see whether the answer holds against what you can actually observe. That is the only version of portability that proves anything.

André runs a community garden and expects underused plots to signal commitment problems. Three rounds of interviews produce a different picture entirely. Some people hired the plot for stress relief through physical work. Others hired it for the neighbor in the adjacent row, a specific person whose presence made the whole activity worth driving across town for. When that neighbor moved away, the plot went fallow. The job evaporated. The dirt was still there. The garden was still there. The person had not failed to commit. The circumstance that made the hire meaningful had quietly ended, and no renewal letter was going to fix that.

Portability works because the structure of human progress is more stable than any individual product category. People keep seeking movement from a constrained current state toward a recognizable better state. The category changes. The pressure, the substitute, and the measure of success are what you have to re-earn with local evidence each time. Portability is proven when local evidence, not category logic, defines the substitute set. Import a conclusion without re-earning the evidence and you are borrowing confidence, not running the method.

The method travels. The conclusions do not.
breakdown.fullRead:
The three-part diagnostic has a simple form: name the circumstance that makes the hire active, describe the progress being sought, and identify the real substitute set. The questions do not change across domains. The answers must come from evidence gathered in the new setting, not from confidence built in the old one.

Chiara is designing software for freelance accountants and expects churn data to point at an invoicing workflow problem. She digs into which features retained users engage most. The CLIENT NOTES field, by a wide margin. Not the invoice templates. Not the payment tracking dashboard. The CLIENT NOTES field, used to log call tone, client mood, and relationship anxiety about a particular account. Retained users are not hiring a billing tool. They are hiring a relationship-anxiety management system that happens to also do billing. The job is legible only because she followed the evidence rather than her prediction.

This is what portability means in practice. You do not carry the answer. You carry the discipline of asking: what situation made this person reach for something, what would a better version of this situation feel like, and what else was this person comparing in that moment. Those questions can survive any domain shift. The answers cannot travel with you.

James evaluates whether to add pronunciation-scoring AI to a language exchange app. The feature addresses a real stated want. Then he looks at cancellation data sorted by what the partner said in the last message. Sessions where the partner wrote something like you are easy to understand have cancellation rates nearly thirty percent lower than sessions where the user scored ninety percent on the accuracy metric. The job the app is hired to do is lower the emotional cost of trying without feeling like a burden. Pronunciation AI answers the stated want and misses the hired job.

Ingrid predicts her color consultation service will lift premium paint sales. At 10:15 in the morning, she watches consultees return to the floor and pick the same mid-range color their neighbor used. Exit interviews repeat the same line: I just needed someone to say I was not going to ruin it. The job is permission to proceed, not color expertise. The consultation earned its value by removing the fear of a visible mistake in front of neighbors.

Kiran adds speed designations to pool lap lanes expecting the fastest swimmers to sort themselves in and improve flow. The fast lane fills instead because the designation signals serious swimmers only, not fastest. Swimmers who are fast but do not identify as serious avoid it even when it is empty. The job served by the designation is social belonging in a peer-defined group. Kiran misread his own fix and built a belonging barrier while solving a flow problem.

Each case holds one structure: someone carried the questions into an unmapped domain, stayed close to observable behavior, and found an answer the category label would never have suggested. The three-part diagnostic travels. The conclusions must be earned each time. That re-earning is not a limitation of the method. It is what the method is.

examples.title: Emily hears why a photo of level 3B beats the valet lot

planSpec.stakes: quality and price gap does not explain the hiring pattern
planSpec.requiredBeat: a frequent traveler reveals the job is certainty of retrieval under stress, not price; a circled photo is the real substitute

examples.scenario: At 10:30 a.m., "Last time you used valet?" Emily asks, recorder between them. The traveler shows a phone photo: concrete pillar marked 3B, her car hood in the corner. "I landed at midnight. Delay. Forty minutes before the last hotel shuttle. That is why I do not valet. I need to know exactly which level my car is on before the elevator opens. Valet cannot promise that after a delay." Emily's notepad says quality gap, price gap. She crosses both out.
examples.whatToDo: Run the three-part diagnostic on the retrieval moment, not the drop-off. Ask what circumstance makes the hire active, what certainty feels like when it works, and what substitute already does that job for the traveler.
examples.whyItMatters: Price and quality are not the competing variables here. The real substitute is a self-park space documented with a phone photo. Valet loses that contest by design, regardless of quality improvements.

examples.title: André finds job evaporation in the underused plots

planSpec.stakes: underuse looks like commitment failure but is job evaporation
planSpec.requiredBeat: interviews reveal three distinct jobs; plots hired for the social belonging job go underused when the neighboring plot-holder moves away

examples.scenario: Warm soil and a hose running in the next row. André, the community garden manager, kneels beside untended beds in late July, plot stakes still bearing April names. Three rounds of interviews reveal three distinct jobs: stress relief through physical work, fresh produce access, and belonging with the neighbor in the adjacent plot. The third group drove across town for one specific person. When that neighbor moved away in June, those plots went fallow within two weeks. Commitment had nothing to do with it.
examples.whatToDo: Segment the plot-holder pool by the job that drove the hire. Treat social-belonging jobs as weather-dependent: when the circumstance that made the hire active changes, plan for turnover, not renewal campaigns.
examples.whyItMatters: Job evaporation is not churn. The gardener did not fail to commit. The circumstance that made the garden worth hiring quietly ended, and no retention letter will reconstruct it.

examples.title: Chiara finds relationship anxiety inside the invoicing software

planSpec.stakes: churn data points away from invoicing and toward an unexpected job
planSpec.requiredBeat: retained users engage the CLIENT NOTES field most; the job is relationship-anxiety management, not billing speed

examples.scenario: Chiara, the product lead, sorts feature engagement by twelve-month retention correlation. The CLIENT NOTES field wins, not invoice templates or payment tracking. Retained users log call tone, client mood, and relationship anxiety. Exit interviews with lapsed users almost never mention billing; several mention not knowing where they stood with their biggest client. The postmortem conclusion: the product's best job is emotional bookkeeping for freelancers afraid a client relationship is quietly going wrong.
examples.whatToDo: Redesign the onboarding sequence to surface CLIENT NOTES early. Frame the product around relationship confidence over billing efficiency in positioning and feature priorities.
examples.whyItMatters: Retained users hired a relationship-anxiety management tool that also handles invoices. A billing-speed roadmap would have spent the next year improving the part of the product that was not driving retention.

examples.title: James weighs pronunciation AI against the cancellation data

planSpec.stakes: pronunciation AI answers the stated want and misses the hired job
planSpec.requiredBeat: sessions where partner says 'you're easy to understand' cancel less than high-accuracy sessions; job is lowering the emotional cost of trying; James faces the decision

examples.scenario: You are James. Top feature request: pronunciation-scoring AI, 340 upvotes. You pull cancellation data sorted by the last partner message before a session ends without rescheduling. Sessions where the partner wrote you are easy to understand cancel thirty percent less often than high-accuracy-score sessions. The accuracy score answers what users asked for. The partner's words answer the fear of being a burden. You must decide which one to build.
examples.whatToDo: Test a lightweight partner-feedback prompt before committing to the pronunciation AI build. Measure whether explicit reassurance from a human partner reduces cancellations more than any accuracy metric improvement.
examples.whyItMatters: The stated want and the hired job are not the same. Pronunciation AI solves what users asked for and misses the emotional cost that drives attrition. Building it without this distinction is a bet on the wrong variable.

examples.title: At 10:15am, Ingrid predicts premium paint, hears permission to proceed

planSpec.stakes: color consultation service expected to lift premium sales
planSpec.requiredBeat: prediction is premium paint sales; reality is mid-range plus the job of permission to proceed; exit line reveals the job

examples.scenario: At 10:15 a.m. Ingrid logs her prediction: premium paint sales will rise among consultees. By noon, five of six consultees return to the floor and pick the same mid-range brand their neighbor used. At the register one buyer says: "You told me it would look fine with our trim. I just needed someone to say I was not going to ruin it." Ingrid reads back through her notes. Every session ended with the same line. The consultation earned its fee by removing the fear of a visible mistake in front of neighbors. Ingrid must decide whether to rebuild the consultation pitch around this job rather than premium paint recommendations.
examples.whatToDo: Reframe the consultation service around the permission job. Train staff to name the anxiety, validate the choice early, and close with a plain statement that the decision is defensible. Track confidence ratings, not paint tier.
examples.whyItMatters: The consultation is not being hired for expertise. It is being hired for the relief that follows a clear, trusted answer from another person. Pricing and staffing built around color knowledge will underserve the actual job.

examples.title: Kiran misreads his own lane fix at the pool

planSpec.domain: public swimming pool lap lane scheduling
planSpec.stakes: speed designations created a belonging problem instead of solving a flow problem
planSpec.requiredBeat: fast lane fills because the designation signals 'serious swimmers only,' not because fastest swimmers self-selected; job is social belonging in a peer-defined lane; Kiran misread his own fix

examples.scenario: This afternoon, Kiran watches the lane distribution from the spectator bench after new speed designations go up. The fast lane is full. Medium-speed swimmers still crowd the middle, even when the fast lane opens. Exit conversations reveal why: the fast lane sign reads serious swimmers only to anyone who is fast but does not claim that identity. The designation created a peer-defined in-group. Kiran fixed a flow problem and built a belonging barrier in the same move. Kiran must decide whether to remove the social signal or add a parallel lane for fast-but-not-serious swimmers.
examples.whatToDo: Reframe the lane criteria around pace over identity. Use observable benchmarks like yards per minute instead of labels like fast or serious, and watch whether the distribution changes.
examples.whyItMatters: The fix addressed speed management and hired a social sorting function nobody asked for. Kiran learned the job by reading the consequence, not the intention, and now has specific evidence for what to change.

questions.prompt: Emily runs the three-part diagnostic on airport valet parking and discovers the substitute is a phone photo of the parking level, not a competing valet service. What does this finding demonstrate about applying the jobs lens to a new domain?
choices: Price may be the real substitute driver because travelers compare valet parking against lower-cost ways to reduce trip anxiety.
The diagnostic produced a result observable in behavior that contradicts the category-based frame, proving portability through evidence, not assumption.
The substitute set is defined by category membership, so the lens must be wrong if no other valet service appears.
questions.explanation: A phone photo of a parking level beats valet because certainty at midnight is the job, not price or quality. That finding only appears by following local evidence instead of assuming category boundaries define the substitute.

questions.prompt: André finds that plots hired for social belonging go fallow when the neighboring plot-holder moves. A garden coordinator wants to fix this with a stronger renewal email campaign. What is the gap in that response?
choices: The renewal message may be arriving too late or sounding too transactional, so better timing and more personal copy could rebuild commitment before plot holders decide not to return.
The garden may need redesigned plots and structured events so belonging is distributed across the community, not dependent on a single neighbor relationship that can disappear.
Renewal campaigns address commitment signals but cannot reconstruct a circumstance that no longer exists; job evaporation requires re-hiring conditions, not re-engagement messaging.
questions.explanation: When the circumstance that made a hire active disappears, no messaging campaign recreates it. The job ended with the neighbor's move. The response needs to address the circumstance gap, not the communication gap.

questions.prompt: Chiara finds that retained freelance accounting software users engage the CLIENT NOTES field most. Her product team wants to add more invoice templates based on this same churn analysis. What is wrong with that conclusion?
choices: The churn analysis points to relationship-anxiety management as the retention driver; a billing-feature roadmap improves the part of the product that is not driving the hiring decision.
The invoice-template conclusion could still be right if CLIENT NOTES are mainly context for billing accuracy, meaning the notes signal richer invoice needs rather than relationship anxiety.
The CLIENT NOTES finding could imply a full relationship dashboard, treating retention as a need for structured client management rather than a lighter notes-based reassurance tool.
questions.explanation: Feature engagement data is evidence of what job is being hired. When retention correlates with CLIENT NOTES over invoice templates, improving billing features responds to assumed demand, not observed hiring behavior.

questions.prompt: James is evaluating a 340-upvote feature request for pronunciation-scoring AI. He finds that sessions where a partner said 'you are easy to understand' cancel thirty percent less often than high-accuracy-score sessions. What should James do before committing the build?
choices: Build the pronunciation AI because 340 upvotes show explicit demand from engaged users, and then use post-launch cancellation data to see whether the requested feature changes retention.
Test whether explicit human reassurance reduces cancellations more than any accuracy metric, using the cancellation data as the success measure, not accuracy improvement.
Run a preference study asking which speaking features users value most, then compare interest in AI scoring against partner feedback before choosing the roadmap priority.
questions.explanation: Upvotes capture the stated want. The cancellation data surfaces the hired job: reducing the emotional cost of trying. Testing reassurance against cancellation rate is the disciplined next step before committing a full AI build.

questions.prompt: Ingrid's color consultation service generates consultees who return to buy mid-range paint instead of premium. An exit interview reveals: 'I just needed someone to say I was not going to ruin it.' Which element of the three-part diagnostic does this quote most directly reveal?
choices: The circumstance that triggered the hire, because it explains when the shopper decided to visit the store.
The substitute set, because it shows what other stores the buyer visited.
The progress being sought: permission to proceed and relief from the anxiety of visible failure in front of neighbors.
questions.explanation: The exit line names the desired end state directly: not expert guidance but the confidence that the decision is defensible. That is the progress dimension of the diagnostic, and it reframes what the consultation service is actually selling.

questions.prompt: Kiran adds speed designations to pool lap lanes and finds that medium-speed swimmers avoid the fast lane even when it is empty, while the fast lane fills with self-identified serious swimmers. He expected a flow outcome. What job did the designation actually serve?
choices: A social belonging job: the designation created a peer-defined in-group that attracted serious-identity swimmers and excluded others regardless of actual pace.
A flow-management job: the labels sorted swimmers by expected pace, and medium swimmers avoided the fast lane because joining it would disrupt the traffic pattern others were relying on.
A safety-signaling job: the fast label warned medium swimmers about higher collision risk, so avoidance reflects self-protection around lane speed rather than social identity.
questions.explanation: The fast lane filled through identity signaling, not pace sorting. The designation hired a social function Kiran did not intend. The distribution only makes sense when read through the belonging job, not the flow problem he was solving.

questions.prompt: A product team hears about the community garden job-evaporation finding and wants to apply it to their subscription app. They write: 'Users who lose their accountability partner will churn.' What is the difference between this claim and a proved job finding?
choices: Subscription data may be stronger proof because churn is a precise timestamped event, while garden observation is messier and harder to compare across participants.

The garden finding was proved by following observable behavior in that specific domain. The app claim is a hypothesis borrowed from analogy; it needs field evidence from that setting to count as proved.
The claims may be equivalent because both describe accountability loss causing disengagement, so the same mechanism can be treated as portable across similar settings.
questions.explanation: Analogy produces hypotheses, not proved jobs. André's finding holds because he followed observable evidence in that specific domain. The app team needs local behavioral data before treating the imported conclusion as actionable.

questions.prompt: A service team is applying the three-part diagnostic to a new domain for the first time. They identify the circumstance and progress dimensions clearly but struggle to name the substitute set. What is the most common reason the substitute set stays hidden?
choices: The substitute set should be left undefined until quantitative surveys confirm the options buyers considered.
Substitutes only exist in consumer markets, so the diagnostic does not apply in B2B settings.
Teams look for substitutes within the product category instead of watching what the buyer actually used before, during, or instead of the hire.
questions.explanation: Category thinking keeps the substitute set narrow. The real substitute often lives outside the category, the way a self-park photo substitutes for valet or a neighbor conversation substitutes for a color expert. Observation of actual behavior before the hire surfaces those options.

questions.prompt: After running the three-part diagnostic in five new domains, a researcher concludes that portability is confirmed because the same three questions always produce an answer. A senior colleague pushes back. What is the strongest version of the colleague's objection?
choices: Producing an answer is not the same as producing a proved answer. Portability requires that conclusions hold against observable evidence in each domain, not just that the question format can be applied.
The diagnostic may need broader domain coverage before portability can be assessed, since five cases might reflect a narrow sample rather than proof that the method travels.
The researcher should publish the five-domain work and let peer review test the method, because independent critique can reveal flaws the original fieldwork missed.
questions.explanation: A diagnostic that always produces an answer can still produce unproved ones. The colleague's objection is that each conclusion must be earned through local evidence. The question form travels; the conclusions must be re-earned every time.

reviewCards.front: You apply the three-part diagnostic in a new domain and get an unexpected answer. What makes that answer a proved finding and not a guess?
reviewCards.back: The answer is proved when it holds against observable evidence gathered in that specific setting: behavior you can watch, substitutes the buyer actually used, and a progress description the buyer recognizes. An unexpected answer backed by local evidence is stronger than a predicted answer backed by confidence from another domain.

reviewCards.front: A user stops engaging with a product after a change in their personal circumstances. What job-theory term describes this pattern?
reviewCards.back: Job evaporation. The circumstance that made the hire active has ended. The user has not failed to commit; the condition that triggered the job no longer exists. Retention efforts that ignore this distinction will treat a structural gap as a messaging problem.

reviewCards.front: A product team finds the CLIENT NOTES field is the strongest retention predictor in their accounting software. How should they use this finding?
reviewCards.back: Treat it as evidence of the real job being hired. The product is being used to manage relationship anxiety, not billing efficiency. Roadmap priorities, onboarding design, and positioning should all be tested against this job before adding more billing features.

reviewCards.front: You identify the circumstance and the progress for a new job. What is the third piece of the diagnostic, and why does it matter for design?
reviewCards.back: The substitute set: what the buyer used, considered, or fell back on before or instead of your product. The substitute defines the real competitive frame and reveals what good enough already looks like from the buyer's point of view. Without it, improvements may target the wrong variable.

reviewCards.front: A fix intended to solve a flow problem creates an unintended belonging barrier. What discipline would have surfaced this risk before implementation?
reviewCards.back: Asking which jobs the change would serve beyond the stated purpose. Changes to shared spaces and shared systems often trigger social jobs nobody planned for. Running the three-part diagnostic on the new arrangement before launch surfaces unintended hiring functions while they are still easy to redesign.

implementationPlan.title: Applying the Job Diagnostic in New Domains
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Apply the three-part diagnostic in a domain you have not mapped before. Name the circumstance that makes the hire active, describe the progress being sought, and identify what the buyer actually compared or used instead. Let observable evidence in that specific domain confirm or revise your prediction before you act on it.

ifThenPlans.plan: If your team is about to apply a finding from another industry to your product, then run the three-part diagnostic in your own domain first and require local evidence before treating the imported conclusion as actionable.

If a health habit you hired for a specific reason stops feeling useful, then name what circumstance originally triggered the hire and whether that circumstance still exists, before replacing the habit with a new one.
If a subscription, membership, or recurring purchase starts to feel hollow, then write the original hiring circumstance and check whether it is still active or has quietly evaporated.

If a shared activity you and someone else both valued starts going unused, then ask whether the circumstance that made it worth hiring together has changed before assuming motivation or commitment is the issue.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one product or service you use regularly in a category unrelated to your work. Write out the three-part diagnostic: the circumstance that makes you hire it, the progress you are seeking, and what you have compared or substituted in the past. If the diagnostic reveals a job different from the product's stated purpose, you have just run a portable field test.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, pick a domain you know nothing about and interview one person who regularly uses a product or service in that domain. Apply the three-part diagnostic strictly: circumstance, progress, substitutes. Record where your prediction was wrong before the evidence came in.

memorableLines.text: Portability is proven when local evidence, not category logic, defines the substitute set.
memorableLines.why: It states what portability actually requires and draws the line between assumption and proof.

memorableLines.text: You do not carry the answer. You carry the discipline of asking: what situation made this person reach for something, what would a better version of this situation feel like, and what else was this person comparing in that moment.
memorableLines.why: It captures the central paradox of portability and names the three questions in one retrievable passage.

memorableLines.text: The category changes. The pressure, the substitute, and the measure of success are what you have to re-earn with local evidence each time.
