memorableLines.why: It names exactly what travels and what must be rebuilt, making the discipline concrete.

chapters.title: Job Hunting
chapters.hook: Camille watches a buyer purchase two adhesive labels plus grout and return them all three days later.
chapters.counterintuition: Teams look for the job in survey responses and feature requests. But actually, buyers translate their struggle into solution language before they speak. The job lives upstream, in the moment where the current answer breaks down before anyone has asked for anything.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name one area where your solution gets returned or improvised around. Write one sentence describing the moment before that: not what failed, but what the person was trying to do. That sentence starts the hunt.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A job hunt starts where current solutions visibly fail the buyer's progress. The evidence lives in returns, workarounds, delays, and the exact moment before someone reaches for the improvised fix.

breakdown.fastRead: Camille does not go looking for a market gap. She goes to investigate a return spike on tile adhesive. What she watches is a buyer holding two adhesive labels side by side, then buying both plus spacers and grout together. Three days later two items come back. The struggling moment is not at the return desk. It is in the tile aisle, where the buyer could not confirm that this combination would work before purchase. The return desk is a downstream symptom. The job lives upstream, in the moment before the mistake.
breakdown.deepRead:
A struggling moment is not a complaint. It is the specific instant where a person's current path to progress stops being reliable enough to follow without risk. The struggling moment comes first, before any feature request, before any complaint, showing up in behavior before it shows up in words.

Lars reviews exit data after extended evening hours at his urgent care clinic fail to grow walk-in volume. He expected the new hours to match what patients said they wanted. The exit data from the competing clinic down the road is more precise. Evening patients did not primarily want more accessible hours. They wanted resolution of a specific question before they drove anywhere: is this serious enough to go to the ER tonight, or can this wait until morning? The struggling moment was uncertainty before arrival. The competitor had added a triage phone line. Lars's extended hours were solving for the right category and the wrong moment.

Good job hunting requires following the moment rather than the category. When surveys ask what customers want, they surface category preference. When observation asks what customers do at the moment their current path fails, it surfaces the job. The gap between those two is where most teams build the wrong thing with total confidence.

Most teams start with features. Job hunting starts with failure.
breakdown.fullRead:
A job hunt begins before any feature gets named. It requires finding the moment where the existing arrangement stops working reliably enough that people start improvising, delaying, tolerating costs, or building workarounds. Those behaviors are stronger signals than any survey because they represent decisions people have already made under actual pressure.

Isabel is at a truck stop conducting exit interviews for a mapping company. She expected GPS dominance to be near-total. A long-haul trucker shows her a road atlas with circled exits. "I know where I am going," he says. "I take the atlas because if the signal drops at mile marker 112, I want the exit I circled six years ago." GPS fails this job by design. It requires signal. The atlas does not. The struggling moment is signal loss at a specific mile marker in the middle of the night, and the job is certainty in that dead zone. Isabel's company is competing against a book with handwritten circles.

David is deciding what to stock at his garden center for spring planting. He has floor observation notes from the previous April. Buyers at full tall flats make fast decisions. Buyers at small sparse flats linger, read the tags twice, sometimes set things down and walk away. He identifies the struggling moment in those lingering patterns: will this look like a started garden by this evening? The job is a plausible start to the season, visible today, when the neighbor can walk by and see that something has begun. Small flats fail this job at any price because the evidence of a start is too thin. The struggling moment is not about money or plant quality. It is about the dread of a bare yard on a Saturday afternoon when the whole street is already blooming.

Frida walks a couple through a wedding venue at 2:15 in the afternoon, expecting the decision points to appear at the AV system and catering packages. The couple returns to the same window three times. Frida stays quiet on the third pass. Finally, one of them says: my parents got married somewhere like this. The job is carrying a specific emotional memory forward into a new event without recreating it exactly. Frida's pricing sheet is organized around the wrong value. The negotiation she prepared is about costs and amenities. The couple is not comparing venues on those dimensions.

Ben runs a children's clothing resale pop-up market and surveys say people come for price. His floor observation does not match. Parents linger longest at the section labeled by occasion: school plays, swim season, winter parties. The struggling moment is the late-night panic before a school play when the right costume does not exist anywhere in the house. The pop-up is not being hired as a discount store. It is being hired as a readiness system for the moments parents cannot plan around. The occasion-labeled tables are not just a display choice. They are evidence of a job that price data cannot describe.

Job hunting is not comfortable because it asks teams to go back to before the solution and sit in the difficulty the buyer was actually in. That position requires resisting the pull toward premature solution language. The struggling moment is not a feature request. It is the raw situation where a person still needs to make progress and has not yet found a reliable path. Everything after that moment is solution. The job lives in the moment itself.

examples.title: Camille traces the return spike to the tile aisle, not the register

planSpec.stakes: return spike investigation points upstream from the register to the aisle
planSpec.requiredBeat: buyer holds two adhesive labels, buys both plus spacers and grout, returns two items three days later; struggling moment is inability to validate combination before purchase; return desk is downstream symptom

examples.scenario: Camille moves through the tile aisle, clipboard in hand, a return spike on adhesive SKU making no sense from register data. She watches a buyer hold two adhesive labels side by side, then add both plus spacers and grout to the cart. Three days later two items come back. Incompatible, the buyer says at the desk. Camille walks back to the aisle: no compatibility guide anywhere near the shelf. The struggling moment is here, not at the return desk. Camille must decide whether to flag this as a label copy problem or an aisle information gap.
examples.whatToDo: Map the combination validation problem in the aisle before redesigning return policy. Ask what a buyer needs at selection to avoid the incompatible purchase, and treat return desk numbers as a count of how often the aisle fails.
examples.whyItMatters: Return data is downstream evidence. The job lives upstream, at the moment a buyer is holding two labels and has no way to confirm they will work together. Solving at the return desk misses the struggling moment entirely.

examples.title: Lars finds the struggling moment before anyone drives to the clinic

planSpec.stakes: extended hours did not grow walk-in volume; struggling moment is uncertainty before arrival
planSpec.requiredBeat: exit data reveals evening patients needed resolution of 'ER or wait' before arriving; struggling moment is pre-arrival uncertainty; competitor added a triage phone line

examples.scenario: Lars pulls the six-month report: extended evening hours, almost no growth in walk-ins. The initiative matched what patients said they wanted. Exit data from the competing clinic three blocks away tells a different story. The difference: a triage phone line. Evening patients called first to answer one question before leaving home: ER tonight, or can this wait? Available hours did not answer that question. The struggling moment was uncertainty before any drive began.
examples.whatToDo: Add a pre-arrival triage line before adjusting hours further. Test whether call volume predicts walk-in conversion and treat calls as the struggling-moment intervention, not a scheduling tool.
examples.whyItMatters: Patients did not want more evening availability. They wanted someone to resolve uncertainty before the drive. The competing clinic found the struggling moment. Lars's extended hours solved for the right category one step too late.

examples.title: Isabel hears why the atlas with circled exits beats the GPS app

planSpec.domain: rural road atlas vs. GPS navigation
planSpec.stakes: trucker's atlas use points to a job GPS fails by design
planSpec.requiredBeat: trucker says atlas is for signal drop at mile marker 112; job is certainty in the dead zone; GPS fails this job by design

examples.scenario: "You have the app," Isabel says at the truck stop table. The trucker taps a dog-eared atlas page with three exits circled in red. "I know where I am going. But if the signal drops at mile marker 112, which it does every time, I want the exit I circled six years ago. The app cannot promise me that at two in the morning." Isabel closes her notebook. Her company has been treating this driver as someone who has not adopted the product. Isabel must decide whether to close the interview or open a new research thread on the dead-zone use case.
examples.whatToDo: Reframe the job around certainty in dead zones, not navigation efficiency. Test whether offline caching of specific previously-marked routes addresses the struggling moment better than general connectivity improvement.
examples.whyItMatters: GPS fails this job by design: it requires signal. The atlas does not. The struggling moment is signal loss at a known location, and no navigation feature improvement will reach a driver whose job is certainty when coverage ends.

examples.title: You stock the garden center before reading the lingering patterns

planSpec.stakes: stocking decision misses the struggling moment visible in floor observation
planSpec.requiredBeat: buyers linger at small sparse flats and walk away; struggling moment is 'will this look like a started garden today'; small flats fail this job at any price; David faces the stocking decision

examples.scenario: You are David. Spring order deadline tomorrow. Your April observation notes show buyers at full tall flats deciding fast; buyers at small sparse flats reading tags twice, setting things down, leaving. One exit note: I just needed it to look like something had already started. You have priced the small flats competitively and placed them at the front. They still do not sell. The tall flats can deliver a visible start by this evening. The small flats cannot. You are looking at the order form. You must choose whether to shift the balance toward the tall flats based on what the exit notes showed.
examples.whatToDo: Shift the stocking mix toward tall flats for the first weeks of spring. Frame the decision around what the yard looks like tonight, not in six weeks. Track the lingering-to-leaving ratio as a struggling-moment indicator.
examples.whyItMatters: The struggling moment is the dread of a bare yard on a Saturday afternoon when the street is already showing color. Price has nothing to do with it. Small flats fail the job regardless of cost because the visible start is not there.

examples.title: At 2:15pm, Frida predicts the AV decision and hears a different job at the window

planSpec.stakes: AV and catering expected to be decision points; real job is carrying an emotional memory forward
planSpec.requiredBeat: at 2:15pm, Frida walks couple through; they return to same window three times; reveal is emotional memory job; pricing sheet organized around wrong value

examples.scenario: At 2:15 p.m. Frida notes her prediction: the couple will ask about AV and catering. She has walked nineteen couples through and the conversation always lands there. This couple asks about ceiling height, then goes quiet. They return to the east-facing window once, then again, then a third time. Frida stays silent on the third pass. One of them says: my parents got married somewhere like this. Frida looks at her pricing sheet. None of those columns holds what just happened. Frida must decide whether to step away from the sheet and ask a different kind of question.
examples.whatToDo: Ask one early question that surfaces emotional memory anchors before the formal tour. Let that answer reorganize what you emphasize, not the capacity and catering packages.
examples.whyItMatters: The couple is not comparing venues on catering or AV. The job is carrying an emotional memory forward without recreating it exactly. A negotiation built around the wrong dimensions will feel like it is solving the wrong problem.

examples.title: Ben watches parents linger at the occasion tables, not the price signs

planSpec.stakes: survey says price; observation says occasion readiness; struggling moment is pre-event panic
planSpec.requiredBeat: parents linger at occasion-labeled section; struggling moment is 'avoid 10pm panic before school play'; pop-up is hired as a readiness system

examples.scenario: Folded tables, labeled bins, fabric-softener smell on the donated coats. Ben watches from the corner. Price signs at every table; parents look and keep moving. Longest dwell time by far is at one section: school plays, swim season, winter parties. A father lifts a costume tunic, checks the size twice, carries it to three other tables, comes back, buys it. In the exit line: I did not think you would have this. I stayed up until midnight last year looking for one. Ben must decide whether to reorganize the entire market by occasion or keep price as the primary display logic.
examples.whatToDo: Reorganize around occasion timing over price tiers. Promote occasion sections before each seasonal event and track dwell time as a leading indicator of which jobs are most active at that moment.
examples.whyItMatters: The struggling moment is the ten p.m. panic before a school event. The pop-up is hired as a readiness system, not a discount shop. Occasion availability is what brought the father back to the tunic three times. Price was not the variable.

questions.prompt: Camille investigates a return spike on tile adhesive and discovers the struggling moment is in the tile aisle, not at the return desk. What does this finding change about how the problem should be addressed?
choices: Change the return policy so buyers feel safer committing, because a longer and easier return window reduces the penalty when the adhesive choice turns out wrong.
Discontinue the weak adhesive SKUs, because returns clustered around products that likely underperform, making product quality the driver of the spike.
The intervention belongs in the aisle, at the moment buyers cannot validate a combination will work before committing, not downstream at the return desk.
questions.explanation: Return data is downstream evidence that the aisle failed a buyer at the moment of selection. Addressing the return policy leaves the struggling moment untouched. The job hunt points to the aisle as the right location for intervention.

questions.prompt: Lars extends clinic hours to match what patients said they wanted in surveys. Walk-in volume does not grow. Exit data reveals the struggling moment was uncertainty before the drive, not inconvenient hours. What does this tell us about survey-based job discovery?
choices: Patients asked for extended hours because they could imagine that solution. The actual struggling moment, pre-arrival uncertainty, was not visible from inside the current arrangement until exit data surfaced it.
The survey was valid but the hours change needs more time and better promotion, because patients may take months to adjust clinic habits after scheduling changes are introduced.
The exit data may be biased toward people who did not use Lars's clinic and miss patients who came successfully, so he should survey the full population before abandoning the hours conclusion.
questions.explanation: Patients expressed a preference they could imagine. The actual job was pre-arrival uncertainty, which only appeared in data about what happened before the patient decided to drive anywhere. Surveys surface imagined solutions; the struggling moment lives upstream of that language.

questions.prompt: Isabel finds that a long-haul trucker uses a road atlas with circled exits for signal-dead zones, not for navigation. A product manager wants to add more offline route caching to the GPS app. What should the manager test first?
choices: Validate the segment size first, because a signal-dead-zone certainty job may be too niche to justify feature work for a GPS product serving many drivers.
Whether offline caching of specific previously-circled routes addresses the certainty job at signal-dead locations better than full-region offline maps.
Add full offline maps first, because broad regional coverage serves the circled-route use case while also helping travelers in other connectivity gaps.
questions.explanation: The struggling moment is signal loss at a specific known mile marker, not general navigation gaps. Full-region offline maps are a category solution. The test should match the job's precision: the exit already marked, reliably available, at mile 112.

questions.prompt: David's floor observation shows that buyers linger and walk away from small sparse flats but buy full tall flats quickly. A vendor argues that lowering prices on small flats will improve conversion. What is wrong with that argument?
choices: The price argument could be right if lingering reflects value comparison: buyers inspect the small flats, calculate price per plant against the taller option, and leave when the math feels poor.

The tall-flat preference may reflect brand recognition and planting confidence rather than a progress job, so clearer labels and growth guidance on small flats could close the trust gap without changing prices.

The lingering and walking away shows the small flat fails the job of a visible start to the season. Price reduction cannot make the yard look like something has already started by this evening, which is the progress the buyer is seeking.
questions.explanation: The struggling moment is the dread of a bare yard on a Saturday afternoon. Price is not the variable preventing a small flat from solving that job. The buyer needs something that looks started now, and small flats cannot deliver that regardless of cost.

questions.prompt: Frida prepares a pricing sheet organized by catering packages and AV tiers before a venue showing. The couple returns to the same window three times and mentions their parents' wedding. What signal in this interaction suggests Frida's pricing sheet addresses the wrong job?
choices: The couple returned to the window three times unprompted, and the only explanation they offered was an emotional memory anchor. The repeated behavior reveals a job that none of the pricing dimensions can hold.
The repeated window visits may signal aesthetic approval rather than an emotional job, meaning the couple has found the right space and now needs the pricing sheet to structure the purchase.
The memory comment may be social pleasantry rather than evidence of a hiring job, while catering and AV remain the real decision drivers because couples often rank those categories first.
questions.explanation: Unprompted repeated behavior at a specific spot is observable job evidence. The couple was not evaluating catering or AV at the window. The emotional memory job is absent from Frida's sheet, and no package discount reaches that gap.

questions.prompt: Ben's pop-up survey says parents come for price. His floor observation shows the longest dwell time at occasion-labeled sections. Which data source should drive the layout decision, and why?
choices: The survey should drive layout because it captures a larger, more representative sample than one floor observation and better reflects the whole customer base.
The floor observation, because dwell time at specific sections is behavior under actual buying pressure, not a stated preference about why the buyer came.
Both signals should shape the layout: price sections near the entrance for stated motivations and occasion sections mid-floor where dwell time is strongest.
questions.explanation: Survey responses reflect what buyers can articulate. Dwell time under buying pressure shows what they actually do when a job is active. The occasion-section behavior shows the readiness job in motion, which a price-preference survey cannot surface.

questions.prompt: A team is trying to identify the struggling moment for their product. They have customer complaints, feature requests, and cancellation data. Which source is most likely to surface the struggling moment, not a downstream symptom?
choices: Feature requests are closest because users file them during use, so they can reveal the moment a missing capability interrupts progress more directly than complaints.
Complaint volume by category is more reliable because aggregation across many users reduces individual interpretation bias and exposes the biggest frustration clusters.
Cancellation data filtered for the specific action or event that happened immediately before the decision to leave, not the stated reason given at cancel.
questions.explanation: Feature requests and complaint categories are solution language. The struggling moment appears in the specific action just before a switch decision, before the buyer translated the struggle into a request. Pre-cancellation behavior is closest to the raw moment.

questions.prompt: A product team is debating whether to run a job hunt by conducting interviews or by observing floor behavior. A colleague says interviews are more efficient because they produce direct answers. What is the strongest argument against relying only on interviews?
choices: Buyers translate their struggling moment into solution language before they speak. Interviews capture the translated version. Observation catches behavior at the moment the translation has not yet happened.
Better interview design can solve the translation problem, because skilled follow-up questions about the moment before the request can push past solution language to the underlying struggle.
Observation fits consumer settings, but interviews may be better for B2B products where the struggling moment happens inside private organizational routines that teams cannot easily watch.
questions.explanation: The core problem is translation. By the time a buyer is answering an interview question, the raw struggling moment has become a feature request, a preference, or a complaint. Floor observation and behavioral data catch the pre-translation moment, which is where the job lives.

questions.prompt: After running a job hunt across four domains, a team concludes that struggling moments always involve some form of uncertainty before a commitment. A senior researcher calls this a useful hypothesis. What would elevate it to a proved finding?
choices: A large survey asking buyers to rate pre-purchase uncertainty could confirm the pattern statistically across domains and make the finding more generalizable.
Testing the uncertainty pattern against behavioral evidence in each specific domain and identifying the workaround buyers already use to manage that uncertainty before purchasing.
Doubling the job hunt from four domains to eight would show broader replication and give the team enough range to treat the uncertainty pattern as proved.
questions.explanation: A cross-domain pattern is a hypothesis until grounded in domain-specific behavioral evidence. The uncertainty claim needs observable workarounds or substitutes in each setting. Survey ratings produce correlation, not a causal struggling moment.

reviewCards.front: A return spike shows up in your data. What is the first job-hunting move?
reviewCards.back: Go upstream from the return desk to the moment before purchase. Find the exact point where the buyer could not validate a decision before committing. The return is a downstream count of how often that upstream moment fails. The intervention belongs at the moment, not the desk.

reviewCards.front: Customers asked for extended hours. You added them. Volume did not grow. What question should you have asked before the build?
reviewCards.back: What is the specific moment where the current arrangement stops being reliable enough for the buyer to act? Extended hours solve for availability. If the real struggling moment is uncertainty before arrival, availability improvements will not reach it. The job hunt has to find the moment before it names the solution.

reviewCards.front: A buyer keeps using an old workaround instead of your product. What does the workaround contain that your product does not?
reviewCards.back: The workaround holds the buyer's solution to the specific struggling moment. It may be slower, uglier, and less capable than your product on every stated dimension. But it does something your product does not do at the moment that matters most. The workaround is a free diagnostic of the real job.

reviewCards.front: Survey data says buyers come for price. Floor observation shows they linger at occasion-labeled sections. Which source do you trust for the job hunt, and why?
reviewCards.back: Trust the floor observation. Survey responses capture what buyers can articulate after the fact. Dwell time under actual buying pressure shows behavior before translation. The job lives in the behavior, not the explanation buyers give when asked to reflect on it.

reviewCards.front: A team says every inconvenience is a potential job. How do you separate a job from noise?
reviewCards.back: A job has four markers: a specific circumstance, a repeated pattern of behavior under that circumstance, a real substitute or workaround the buyer already uses, and a cost the buyer is already paying to make progress. Curiosity, mild annoyance, and passing preferences do not have all four. A job does.

implementationPlan.title: Locating the Struggling Moment Before Solutions
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Before naming any feature or solution, locate the struggling moment: the specific instant where the buyer's current path to progress stops being reliable enough to follow without risk. The evidence for that moment lives in returns, workarounds, delays, and the behavior that happens just before a buyer improvises or walks away.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a feature request lands on your roadmap, then write one sentence describing the specific moment before a buyer would make that request, naming what they were trying to do when the current arrangement stopped working.
If a health habit is getting abandoned or replaced with an improvised fix, then write the exact moment where the current routine stops working before deciding what to replace it with.

If a recurring purchase keeps feeling like the wrong choice even after trying several options, then write the moment before the purchase where the previous solution failed, and name what you were actually trying to do there.
If a shared system or routine keeps breaking down, then describe the specific moment where the arrangement stops working for the person who exits it first, before proposing a new structure.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, find one area in your work where a product gets returned, abandoned, or replaced by a workaround. Write one sentence describing the moment before that happens: not what went wrong with the product, but what the buyer was trying to do at that specific instant. That sentence is the start of a job hunt.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, observe instead of asking. Watch someone using a product or service in its natural setting without explaining what you are looking for. Write down the moment when their current path stops looking smooth. Note any workaround, pause, backup option, or alternative they reach for. That observation is your raw job data.

memorableLines.text: The return desk is a downstream symptom. The job lives upstream, in the moment before the mistake.
memorableLines.why: It relocates where the problem actually lives, changing where teams should look for evidence.

memorableLines.text: The struggling moment is not a feature request. It is the raw situation where a person still needs to make progress and has not yet found a reliable path.
memorableLines.why: It draws the line between the job and all the solution language that comes after it.

memorableLines.text: The job lives in the moment itself.
memorableLines.why: Short, precise, and impossible to misread. It anchors the entire chapter's discipline in one line.

chapters.title: How to Hear What Your Customers Don't Say
chapters.hook: Rachel's UX upgrade launches. The ticket portal stays stuck at 37%.
chapters.counterintuition: Listening for the job means listening past the stated preference. When words and behavior diverge, behavior carries the stronger evidence. In fact, behavior is usually held in place by forces the customer never volunteers.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick a customer who praised your product and then left. Write one sentence each for push, pull, habit, and anxiety. If the anxiety sentence stays blank, that is the force you have not yet listened for.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Four forces govern every switch: push and pull move customers toward change while habit and anxiety push back. When the holding pair dominates, improving pull does not close the gap.

breakdown.fastRead:
Rachel's portal improvements go live. The ticket rate barely moves. Employees say it looks better. They still call IT.

Four forces govern every switch. Push: the situation is bad enough to prompt action. Pull: the new option looks better. Habit: the existing routine feels safe. Anxiety: the new path carries unknown risk. Push and pull favor switching. Habit and anxiety favor staying. A buyer who praised the new tool and still rescheduled four times is not confused, because push and pull are real, but so are habit and anxiety, and the pair on the holding side can outweigh the pair on the switching side.

Customers volunteer push and pull. Habit and anxiety need a different kind of listening.
breakdown.deepRead:
A four-force map starts with the gap between what customers say and what they do. That gap is not irrationality. It is a signal that at least one force is operating below the surface.

Push is the easiest to hear. Customers describe what is slow, painful, or expensive. The IT employee who still calls instead of filing a ticket feels some push. That is why the portal was considered at all.

Pull is nearly as visible. The new portal loads fast and tracks status. Pull brought them to the demo or the first login.

Habit is harder. Calling IT feels normal, not habitual, even after four years. Habit does not feel like a choice from the inside. Ask what would disappear from the day if this changed. Anything the customer names without thinking is probably wired into routine.

Anxiety is the hardest. At 6:14 a.m., Mathieu reviews booking data: first-session attendance sits at 22% despite healthy booking volume. Patients book to relieve the anxiety of not having sought help yet. Once that job is done, the internal pressure eases. The habit of functioning adequately fills the gap. The session becomes optional. Habit and anxiety together outweigh the push that generated the booking.

For the IT portal, the anxiety is specific. A ticket creates a timestamp. Calling IT leaves no trace. Rachel's redesign made the pull stronger but left the anxiety intact. The holding forces were never addressed, so the behavior did not change.

Four-force listening is not a survey. It is an interview discipline that creates space for the holding forces to surface. Ask about last time, not next time. Ask what felt risky. Ask what routine would break if the switch succeeded. Those questions reach the forces customers do not volunteer on their own.
breakdown.fullRead:
Every team that improves a product and watches adoption stall is missing at least one of the Four Forces of Progress. The product may be objectively better. The pull may be real. The push may be strong enough to generate trials. And still nothing shifts. The explanation almost always lives in the holding pair: habit and anxiety.

Habit is invisible to the people who hold it. Paula watches customers linger at her new warmth-rating comparison board and then leave without buying. They came in because their current bag was too cold. That push is genuine. The board increased the pull by making performance differences visible. But standing at the board made the cost-of-overbuy explicit. The board that clarified performance simultaneously amplified the anxiety of making an expensive mistake. Customers left knowing more and buying less.

Information that increases pull can also make the cost of an error more salient, which raises anxiety. A four-force map helps a team predict which change will affect which force before shipping. Paula's board is proof that a helpful move can amplify the force it was meant to overcome.

Anxiety tends to be masked by polite language. Customers say they need to think about it, compare options, or revisit next quarter. Almost none say they are afraid the ticket system will be used against them, or that the dietary station marks them as different during the only unscripted thirty minutes of the day.

Petra watches the special-diet station sit at under 30% usage while employees who need it eat ordinary food with their teams. Push is real. Pull is real. But the habit of eating with any colleague on any given day is the social texture of the work day, and the anxiety of being visibly separated from that texture blocks the hire. Expanding the station adds more pull without touching either holding force.

Aman hears this in a notary context. Walk-in hours are open. Appointment-only competitors are fuller. Listening reveals an anxiety: what if the document is filled in wrong and the visit counts for nothing? The appointment is hired not for the notarization but for the certainty that the document will be accepted. Walk-in implies improvisation. Appointment implies the notary has been briefed. The job includes a pre-visit protocol, not just a stamp.

Luke hears it in a financial literacy intake. The functional job stated at the outset masks the social job underneath. Push is household shame. Pull is looking competent in a partner's eyes. But the habit of avoiding the money conversation feels like stability, and the anxiety that a budget will reveal how bad things actually are blocks the intake.

Once a team maps all four forces, the product question changes. It is no longer what makes the product better. It is which force is holding customers in place, and what change would address that force without accidentally amplifying another.

The four-force map is also a listening protocol. In every customer conversation, a researcher can track which force is being described. When push and pull dominate and holding forces are absent, the team has an incomplete picture. The most useful moment in any interview is when a customer describes the habit they would lose or the risk they are not willing to take. That is the place where behavior actually lives.

The conversation that surfaces the holding forces bears no resemblance to a market research interview. Someone finally asked the question the customer had been waiting to answer.

examples.title: Rachel's IT portal stalls at 37% after a full UX upgrade

planSpec.stakes: adoption flat despite real improvement
planSpec.requiredBeat: IT portal plateaued at 37%. Employees don't submit tickets because written records feel like evidence they caused the problem. Habit plus anxiety outweigh the pull. Rachel's UX improvement addresses none of the holding forces.

examples.scenario: Three months after launch, Rachel sits at her desk with the adoption dashboard open. The portal is cleaner, faster, and better on mobile. The submitted-ticket rate has moved from 34% to 37%. Exit interviews from the previous quarter come back to one phrase in different forms: employees call IT because a phone call disappears. A ticket stays. The written record is evidence. Habit and anxiety were never touched by the redesign. The pull improved. The holding forces stayed exactly where they were.
examples.whatToDo: Map habit and anxiety before the next release. Ask what calling protects and what writing risks. Design a path where the ticket record is visible to the employee, not only to IT.
examples.whyItMatters: A product can improve on every technical measure while adoption stalls because the dominant force is anxiety, not usability. Rachel's team optimized the pull while the holding forces remained untouched.

examples.title: Mathieu finds that the booking is hired to end the decision, not start the session

planSpec.stakes: completion rate at 22% despite strong booking volume
planSpec.requiredBeat: At 6:14am, bookings are high but first-session attendance is 22%. Patients book to relieve the anxiety of not-having-sought-help-yet. The booking resolves the decision anxiety. Habit: feeling better after deciding delays the first session.

examples.scenario: At 6:14 a.m., Mathieu expects the shortfall to trace to scheduling friction. Bookings are healthy. First-session attendance is 22%. The gap is not in the reminder sequence. Patients book, feel the relief of having decided, and find that urgency softens. The booking was hired to end the anxiety of not having sought help. Once that job is done, the habit of functioning adequately fills the gap. The session stays on the calendar as a future option, not an urgent appointment. Mathieu must decide whether to redesign the reminder sequence or investigate the booking step itself.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the job of booking from the job of attending. Test a brief contact that reactivates the original push without creating a new obligation. Measure the gap before adjusting the product.
examples.whyItMatters: When the booking is hired to relieve the anxiety of not deciding, it competes with the session and blocks it. Habit and anxiety together can turn a healthy funnel into a dead end between two steps.

examples.title: Paula's comparison board increases dwell time and reduces sales

planSpec.domain: camping and outdoor gear sleeping bag display
planSpec.stakes: information that strengthens pull amplifies anxiety
planSpec.requiredBeat: Paula adds a warmth-rating comparison board. Customers spend more time but buy less. Floor observation maps all four forces. The comparison board amplified anxiety by making the cost-of-overbuy explicit.

examples.scenario: Nylon and dried mud fill the display wall's scent. This afternoon, Paula watches two customers work through the warmth-rating board for eleven minutes, then leave. Push: their current bag was too cold. Pull: the board clarifies performance. But four tiers and seven price points made the cost-of-overbuy explicit. Habit kept the old bag alive as mostly adequate. The customer leaves knowing more and buying nothing. Paula must decide whether the board stays or changes.
examples.whatToDo: Reframe the board around trip type over spec tier. Help customers match a trip description to a bag. That keeps pull intact while reducing the overbuy anxiety the ratings table was amplifying.
examples.whyItMatters: Transparency about performance can raise the anxiety of a wrong decision faster than it raises the pull of the right one. Four-force thinking predicts that outcome before the board goes up.

examples.title: Luke hears the real job inside a budget intake

planSpec.stakes: functional job masks the social job
planSpec.requiredBeat: Functional job masks social job. Push: household shame. Pull: competence in partner's eyes. Habit: avoiding the money conversation. Anxiety: the budget reveals how bad it actually is.

examples.scenario: "I don't actually need a budget," the client says. "I need my husband to stop looking at me like I don't understand money." Luke writes it down verbatim. The intake form covers income and debt. None of those fields hold what just walked in. Push: the look across the dinner table. Pull: walking into that conversation differently. Habit: years of avoiding the money talk. Anxiety: what the budget will show once it is real on paper. Luke must decide whether to continue with the intake form or set it aside.
examples.whatToDo: Hold the intake form and ask what a good outcome would feel like in the household, not just the account. If the job is relational credibility, the coaching design has to address the social dimension before the spreadsheet is useful.
examples.whyItMatters: A budget intake designed for functional progress leaves the dominant job unaddressed. Luke can build a technically sound plan that the client never uses because it solved the wrong four forces.

examples.title: Petra faces the special-diet station expansion while holding forces remain untouched

planSpec.stakes: expansion addresses pull without touching holding forces
planSpec.requiredBeat: Special-diet station usage below 30% of target group. Interviews: using the designated station marks them as different during the only casual social time of the work day. Push and pull are real but habit plus anxiety block the hire. Petra faces the expansion decision.

examples.scenario: Usage is at 28%. You have the interview notes. The phrase that repeats is a version of: lunch is the one time I walk to whoever I want, and the station makes that harder. Push is real. Pull is real. But the habit of eating with any colleague is the social texture of the day. The anxiety of being visibly separated during the only unstructured thirty minutes is blocking the hire. Petra's expansion adds more options at the same designated space. You are holding the proposal and must decide whether to approve it, revise it, or return it with a question.
examples.whatToDo: Return the proposal with one question: which force does the expanded station address? If the answer is pull, test whether a distributed option reaches the job that a designated space cannot.
examples.whyItMatters: Expanding a product that serves push and pull well does not help when the barrier is habit and anxiety. Petra's decision is not about the food. It is about which force is actually dominant.

examples.title: Aman learns that the appointment is hired for certainty, not convenience

planSpec.stakes: walk-in availability does not address the dominant anxiety
planSpec.requiredBeat: Walk-in hours are open but appointment-only competitors are fuller. Anxiety: what if I fill it in wrong and have to come back? The appointment is hired for certainty that the document will be valid. Walk-in implies improvisation; appointment implies the notary has been briefed.

examples.scenario: Ink smell and the tick of the wall clock fill Aman's office at 2:15 p.m. Two chairs sit open. The competitor two blocks north has a three-day wait. Aman asks customers who book why they chose an appointment. The answer repeats in different words: they are afraid of filling something in wrong and coming back. The appointment is hired for the confidence that the document will be valid on arrival. Walk-in implies improvisation. Appointment implies the notary has been briefed. Aman must decide whether to add a pre-visit confirmation protocol or continue with walk-in availability.
examples.whatToDo: Build the confirmation into a pre-visit protocol: one message confirming document type, requirements, and what to bring. That message is the actual product. The stamp is secondary.
examples.whyItMatters: When the dominant force is anxiety about document validity, walk-in availability is not an advantage. It signals that no one has been briefed. The job includes certainty before arrival, and Aman's office was only selling access.

questions.prompt: An employee praises the new ticketing portal in a survey but continues calling IT every time an issue appears. Which explanation best fits a four-force analysis of this behavior?
choices: Habit and anxiety are holding the old behavior in place more strongly than push and pull are driving the switch.
The employee has not had time to read the onboarding documentation.
The portal's visual design is insufficiently differentiated from the previous system.
questions.explanation: Stated preference and observed behavior diverge when holding forces dominate. The employee's continued phone calls show that habit and anxiety outweigh pull, regardless of what the survey captured.

questions.prompt: A team sees strong booking volume for an online therapy service but only 22% of bookers attend their first session. Applying four-force thinking, what is the most likely explanation?
choices: The reminder sequence is failing because post-booking communication does not sustain the motivation that produced the appointment, so attendance drops before session day.
The booking is being hired to resolve the anxiety of not having sought help, so the internal pressure that drove the booking eases before the session date.
The issue is platform trust: after booking, users worry a digital-first session will feel unsafe, so a human phone check-in would preserve commitment.
questions.explanation: When the act of booking completes the job of relieving decision anxiety, the session no longer carries urgency. The habit of functioning adequately fills the gap and the appointment becomes optional.

questions.prompt: Paula adds a detailed warmth-rating comparison board to a sleeping bag display. Dwell time increases but sales drop. Which four-force dynamic best explains the outcome?
choices: The board created pull and the sales drop may be temporary, because better-informed shoppers could return later through a channel the store did not track.
The board created decision fatigue by showing too many ratings at once, so simplifying the comparison to two key dimensions would recover sales.
The board strengthened pull by clarifying performance but simultaneously amplified the anxiety of buying the wrong rating at too high a price.
questions.explanation: Information that increases pull can also make the cost of an error more salient, raising anxiety. A four-force map would have predicted that making price tiers explicit could activate the overbuy fear already holding buyers back.

questions.prompt: A client opening a financial literacy intake says she does not need a budget; she needs her husband to stop looking at her like she does not understand money. What does this reveal about the job?
choices: The functional job of creating a budget masks a social job: gaining credibility within the household relationship.
The client is deflecting because she is not ready to engage with the intake process.
The program should add a couples financial planning module to address co-management challenges.
questions.explanation: The client's words name a social job directly. Push is relational shame, pull is household credibility, and anxiety is that the budget will confirm the underlying problem instead of resolving it.

questions.prompt: A corporate special-diet station sits at 28% usage among eligible employees. Interviews reveal that using the station marks employees as visibly different during the only informal social period of the day. Which action best addresses the dominant holding force?
choices: Expand the station to offer a wider variety so that more dietary preferences are covered.
Move the station closer to the main serving area to reduce the physical distance employees must travel.
Test a distributed or integrated option that removes the social marking without reducing the dietary safety the station provides.
questions.explanation: The dominant force is the anxiety of social separation during a valued routine. More options at the same station add pull without touching the holding force. Integration targets the anxiety directly.

questions.prompt: Aman's walk-in notary office has open chairs while appointment-only competitors are booked three days out. Customer interviews reveal fear of filling in a document incorrectly and having to return. What does this tell you about the dominant job?
choices: Appointment availability is primarily a scheduling preference and has little bearing on the core service.
The competitor's higher volume proves that their pricing model is more competitive than Aman's.
The appointment is hired for the certainty that the document will be valid, and walk-in hours signal improvisation, not preparation.
questions.explanation: The customer's anxiety is about document validity, not access. The appointment signals a briefed professional. Walk-in access removes that signal. The job is pre-visit certainty, not same-day availability.

questions.prompt: A team is conducting customer interviews after an adoption plateau. Customers freely describe what frustrated them about the old product and what attracted them to the new one. What is most likely missing from the picture?
choices: Push and pull are well represented but habit and anxiety are unlikely to surface unless the researcher creates space for them explicitly.
The team needs more interviews from a wider demographic range to confirm the pattern.
The interview data is sufficient because customers have already identified the key switching factors.
questions.explanation: Customers volunteer push and pull naturally because those forces feel like reasons. Habit rarely feels like a choice and anxiety is uncomfortable to admit. Researchers have to create conditions where holding forces can surface.

questions.prompt: A product team ships a significant usability improvement. Survey satisfaction scores rise. Repeat usage does not change. Which four-force conclusion is most defensible?
choices: Repeat usage is typically a lagging indicator and the team should wait another quarter before drawing conclusions.
The improvement addressed pull but the dominant barrier was likely habit or anxiety, which the usability change left intact.
Satisfaction and usage are independent metrics and should not be compared in the same analysis.
questions.explanation: Satisfaction rising while behavior stays flat is the clearest evidence that pull improved while a holding force remained dominant. The team improved the wrong side of the four-force map.

questions.prompt: During a customer interview, a researcher hears a client describe the habit they would lose if they switched and the specific risk they are not willing to take. What is the researcher listening to?
choices: The researcher is hearing objections for competitive positioning, since the habit and risk give marketing exact concerns to answer in sales materials.
The holding forces: the pair of habit and anxiety that most directly explains why behavior has not changed despite real push and pull.
The researcher is hearing feature gaps, because the lost habit names what the current product does and the risk points to a missing capability.
questions.explanation: The moment a customer names a habit that would disappear or an anxiety they are protecting is the moment the researcher has found where behavior actually lives. Those are the holding forces the four-force model is designed to surface.

reviewCards.front: A customer says your product is better but keeps using the old one. Which force pair are you most likely underestimating?
reviewCards.back: Habit and anxiety. Pull may be real and push may exist, but the holding pair is keeping behavior in place. Ask what the old routine protects and what the new path risks before changing the product.

reviewCards.front: Why do customers rarely volunteer holding forces in interviews?
reviewCards.back: Habit does not feel like a choice from the inside, and anxiety is uncomfortable to admit. Researchers have to create space by asking about last time, asking what feels risky, and asking what routine would break if the switch succeeded.

reviewCards.front: A change makes your product more attractive and also stalls sales. What four-force dynamic should you check first?
reviewCards.back: Check whether the same change that strengthened pull also amplified anxiety. Making performance differences explicit can raise the cost of being wrong just as fast as it raises the appeal of being right.

reviewCards.front: What does it mean when words and behavior diverge in customer data?
reviewCards.back: It means at least one force is operating below the surface of the stated preference. Behavior carries the stronger evidence. The gap between what customers say and what they do is the map to the dominant force.

reviewCards.front: A product team maps push and pull accurately but adoption stays flat. What is the most likely gap in their analysis?
reviewCards.back: They have mapped the switching forces but not the holding forces. Habit and anxiety together can outweigh strong push and pull. The team needs to name the routine being disrupted and the risk being triggered.

implementationPlan.title: Mapping All Four Adoption Forces
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Map all four forces before diagnosing an adoption problem. The skill is to name the push, pull, habit, and anxiety separately, then identify which force is dominant in the current behavior rather than in the stated preference.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a product improvement ships and adoption does not move, then map all four forces before scoping the next release. Name the habit being disrupted and the anxiety being triggered before building anything new.

If you praise a new routine and then return to the old one, then write the habit the old routine holds and the anxiety the new one triggers. Naming both forces out loud is the first step to addressing either.

If a decision feels stuck despite obvious logic, then list what you would lose from the current routine and what risk the new path carries. Those two items are the holding forces the logic has not yet answered.
If someone agrees with a suggested change and then does not make it, then ask what the current pattern protects before offering another reason to switch.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, find one situation where you or someone else said something positive and then behaved differently. Write the push, pull, habit, and anxiety for that situation. If the anxiety sentence is blank, that is the force you have not yet listened for.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, conduct one customer or colleague conversation where you explicitly listen for all four forces. After the conversation, write each force in one sentence and identify which pair was dominant.

memorableLines.text: A buyer who praised the new tool and still rescheduled four times is not confused, because push and pull are real, but so are habit and anxiety, and the pair on the holding side can outweigh the pair on the switching side.
memorableLines.why: It names all four forces in one sentence and explains the divergence between stated preference and behavior.

memorableLines.text: Habit does not feel like a choice from the inside.
memorableLines.why: It captures why holding forces are invisible to the people who hold them and why researchers must create space for them.

memorableLines.text: Information that increases pull can also make the cost of an error more salient, which raises anxiety.
memorableLines.why: It captures the counterintuitive dynamic where a helpful change amplifies the force it was meant to overcome.

chapters.title: Building Your Resume
chapters.hook: Sophie expects crisis calls. The data shows something quieter and more trusted.
chapters.counterintuition: Most teams build identity from what they intend to offer. Instead, the market writes a different record through the pattern of repeated hires, and that pattern is often narrower, more specific, and more valuable than the team's stated purpose.
chapters.tryThisNow: List five times your product was rehired. For each, write: circumstance and progress sought. If all five name the same job, that is your earned resume. If they split, you have two products sharing one identity.
chapters.keyTakeaway: An offering earns its resume through repeated hires in similar circumstances. When actual use diverges from stated mission, the earned pattern is the stronger signal to follow.

breakdown.fastRead:
Sophie reviews the crisis text line data expecting intervention to dominate. Repeat contacts cluster outside crisis moments, before hard talks, before stressful weeks. The line has earned a resume as a trusted pre-crisis check-in space. The grant proposal sells crisis intervention. The resume the market wrote is pre-crisis maintenance.

This gap is not a failure. It is a finding. The market has trusted the service with something specific and repeatable. That pattern is the most honest description of what the offering actually does well.

The question before the next grant or expansion: what has the market actually trusted us with, and does our identity reflect that?
breakdown.deepRead:
A resume claim is only as strong as the pattern behind it. One vivid case illustrates a job. Many similar hires in similar circumstances confirm that the market has decided to trust an offering with a specific kind of progress.

Sophie's data shows the pattern clearly. The grant positions the service as crisis intervention. Three cohorts show something narrower. Repeat contacts arrive before hard conversations and high-stakes weeks, not during crisis. The service has earned a resume as a pre-crisis check-in space. That is not what the grant said. It is what the market wrote.

Mikkel faces the same discovery in cycling infrastructure. Paths built for commuters are used heavily for weekend recreation. The earned resume is recreational. Mikkel can argue that the original justification still holds, or acknowledge what the market actually hired.

Catarina sees it in a community college evening program. The career accelerator was designed for skill acquisition. Three cohorts show the same pattern: participants had already decided to change careers. What they needed was a credible step to show family. The job is social proof for a household conversation, not skills. The branding says one thing. The earned resume says another.

In each case, the gap between claimed identity and earned resume is a strategic signal. The claimed identity reflects the team's original intention. The earned resume reflects what buyers have actually decided to rely on. When those diverge, the earned resume is the more useful description of the real competitive position.

The move is to read the pattern with circumstances attached. Who rehired, in what situation, after what pressure, for what progress? A pattern that holds across similar circumstances is a resume line.
breakdown.fullRead:
Teams describe their products from the inside. They name capabilities, audiences, and brand values. Buyers write a different record. They reveal what they trust by returning to an offering when a familiar pressure appears. That return is the vote. Repeated returns in similar circumstances are the resume.

The resume metaphor matters because it is earned. A candidate can claim a skill on paper. A resume is stronger when it shows repeated proof under recognizable conditions. An offering works the same way. One story points toward a possible job. Many similar hires show what buyers rely on. The team should treat that reliance as strategic evidence, not as confirmation the strategy was right.

Chris reviews two years of pet boarding intake surveys and finds that the verbal handoff notes tell a different story. Repeat clients spend almost all verbal time at pickup on separation anxiety behavior, not feeding or exercise. The facility has been hired to manage separation anxiety. The survey measured the wrong job. Two years of repeat clients have written a resume the intake form never asked about.

Anke built a commercial photography studio around architecture work. Repeat bookings come from event coordinators needing post-event documentation for funder reports. The studio has earned a resume as trusted documentary evidence. That job is completely invisible in the marketing. The strongest part of the business has no voice in how it describes itself.

Layla's tool library was built to reduce costs through shared equipment. The highest-repeat borrowers check out modest tools: caulk guns, pipe wrenches, basic items a first-time homeowner might need once. The same person borrows the same tool multiple times. The job is not cost reduction. It is permission to start a task you are not sure how to do, without committing to ownership if it goes wrong. The library's earned resume is enabling the attempt, not saving the money.

These discoveries share a structure. The original design intention is legible in the product. The earned resume is written in the pattern of actual use. When the two diverge, the team faces a decision about which identity to commit to.

The risk of ignoring the earned resume is that the team invests in the claimed identity while the market trusts a different one. If the next expansion is built around crisis intervention, it may miss the job that made the service worth returning to.

The opposite error is equally real. Over-generalizing from a pattern asks the market to trust something unearned. The circumstances have to stay specific. The resume describes a bounded trust, not a license to expand in any direction.

Building the resume as a discipline means three things. Track repeat hires with circumstances attached. Compare the earned resume to the stated identity. Use the earned resume to discipline expansion. Does the proposed move extend a trust the market has granted, or claim a trust the market has not yet written?

An offering earns its identity the same way a professional earns theirs: through repeated proof under pressure. The market does not award identity based on intention. It writes the resume through repeated hires. Reading that record accurately is the work.

examples.title: Sophie's crisis line earns a pre-crisis resume

planSpec.stakes: grant identity diverges from earned usage pattern
planSpec.requiredBeat: At 8:47am, Sophie reviews metrics expecting crisis intervention to dominate. Repeat contacts cluster outside crisis moments. The earned resume is pre-crisis maintenance. The grant proposal has been selling crisis intervention.

examples.scenario: At 8:47 a.m., Sophie pulls up the metrics expecting crisis volume to anchor the story. Repeat contacts cluster elsewhere: before hard conversations, before stressful weeks. Three years of service have built a resume as a trusted pre-crisis check-in space. The grant proposal due Friday calls it crisis intervention. The market has decided to trust something quieter and more sustained. Sophie must decide whether to defend the original framing or renegotiate what the grant is actually funding.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the crisis contacts from the pre-crisis check-in pattern. Describe the earned resume accurately in the grant proposal and measure outcomes that match the actual job, not the originally intended one.
examples.whyItMatters: Funding for crisis intervention may not cover the job the market has actually hired. If Sophie builds the next service expansion around crisis, she may miss the users whose trust built the resume.

examples.title: Mikkel's commuter paths earn a recreational resume

planSpec.stakes: original justification diverges from actual use pattern
planSpec.requiredBeat: The paths were built for commutes. They are heavily used for weekend recreation. Mikkel faces the decision of whether to argue the earned resume or retrofit the data.

examples.scenario: The report lands on Mikkel's desk at 9:15 a.m. "You said commuters," the council liaison says. Weekend recreational traffic is double the weekday commute volume. The paths were built around a commuter justification. The market has written a different resume. Mikkel must decide whether to defend the original framing at the meeting or acknowledge what the paths have earned and build the next phase around that.
examples.whatToDo: Name the earned resume directly. If recreational use is the stronger pattern, the next phase of infrastructure investment should serve that job rather than retrofit it into the original commuter framing.
examples.whyItMatters: Defending a claimed identity against an earned one protects the original story at the cost of the actual opportunity. The market has decided what to trust the paths with. That decision is more useful than the original justification.

examples.title: Catarina's career program earns a social-proof resume

planSpec.stakes: skill branding misses the job three cohorts confirmed
planSpec.requiredBeat: Career accelerator built for skills. Three cohorts show same pattern: people who had already decided to change careers needed a credible step to show family. Job is social proof for a household conversation. Branding says one thing; earned resume says another.

examples.scenario: Catarina reads the third cohort debrief and marks the same observation she marked in cohorts one and two. Participants arrived having already made the career decision. What they needed was a credential they could put on the table in a household conversation. The branding says skills accelerator. The earned resume says I went back to school, which means this is serious. Three cohorts have written the same line. Catarina has a program that has earned a specific trust and is selling something else entirely.
examples.whatToDo: Reframe the program around the job three cohorts confirmed. Design the outcomes, testimonials, and enrollment materials around the household conversation the credential is hired to enable, not the skill it is assumed to deliver.
examples.whyItMatters: A program that earns trust as social proof and markets itself as skills is invisible to the people who most need it and unconvincing to the families it actually helps.

examples.title: Chris discovers the pet boarding intake survey measured the wrong job

planSpec.stakes: two years of repeat data reveal the actual job the survey never asked about
planSpec.requiredBeat: Reviewing two years of intake surveys. Verbal handoff notes tell a different story. Repeat clients spend almost all verbal time on separation anxiety behavior. The facility has been hired to manage separation anxiety. The survey measured the wrong job. Chris faces the survey redesign decision.

examples.scenario: At 8:30 a.m., you review two years of intake surveys alongside the front desk handoff notes. The survey covers feeding, exercise, and medication. The notes cover one topic across repeat clients: how the dog behaved when the owner left, and whether that got better or worse. The facility has been hired to manage separation anxiety. The survey never asked about that job. You must decide whether to adopt Chris's redesign proposal or commission a survey that asks the right question first.
examples.whatToDo: Approve the redesign with a condition: ask about separation anxiety as its own section, track it as an outcome, and design the boarding environment around the job repeat clients confirmed.
examples.whyItMatters: Two years of repeat hires have written a resume the intake form never captured. Chris's redesign is not adding a question. It is finally asking about the job the market already trusted the facility with.

examples.title: Anke's studio earns a documentary evidence resume no one mentions in marketing

planSpec.stakes: strongest job is invisible in marketing
planSpec.requiredBeat: Anke built the studio around architecture and interior photography. Repeat bookings come from event coordinators needing post-event documentation for funder reports. The studio has earned a resume as trusted documentary evidence. Its strongest job is invisible in the marketing.

examples.scenario: Flash powder and fresh gesso scent the studio. Anke sorts eighteen months of invoices by repeat clients. Architecture bookings are one-time. The repeat column fills with event coordinators: post-event documentation for funder reports, proof images for grant accountability. The studio has earned a resume as trusted documentary evidence. That job appears nowhere in the website. Anke must decide whether to update the website to reflect what the market has actually hired the studio for.
examples.whatToDo: Give the earned resume a voice in the marketing. Name the documentary evidence job explicitly, show examples of grant accountability work, and design the intake process around the standards funders use to evaluate proof images.
examples.whyItMatters: The strongest part of Anke's business is invisible to the clients who most need it. The earned resume is not a surprise discovery. It is a competitive position the studio has already built. It just has no name.

examples.title: Layla finds the tool library earns permission to attempt, not cost savings

planSpec.stakes: original cost-sharing mission diverges from actual repeat borrower job
planSpec.requiredBeat: Built to reduce costs by sharing expensive tools. Highest-repeat borrowers consistently check out modest items. Same first-time homeowner borrowing the same basic tool multiple times. Job: permission to start a task you're not sure you know how to do, without committing to owning the tool if it goes wrong.

examples.scenario: Machine oil and sawdust fill the library. This afternoon, Layla sorts circulation records by repeat borrower volume. The highest-repeat column is not expensive tools avoided for cost reasons. It is caulk guns, pipe wrenches, and basic hand tools from the same addresses. The same person rents a caulk gun three times in one year. The job is not cost avoidance. It is permission to start a repair you are not confident about, without committing to the tool if it goes wrong. Layla must decide whether to reframe the lending program around confidence rather than cost savings.
examples.whatToDo: Redesign the library's description around the earned resume. Name the first-attempt job explicitly in materials, add brief how-to guidance with each modest tool, and measure outcomes around completed first repairs over cost savings.
examples.whyItMatters: The library was built to serve cost-conscious borrowers. It has earned a resume with people who need confidence, not savings. Those are different jobs with different success measures and different expansion paths.

questions.prompt: Sophie reviews usage data for a crisis text line and finds that repeat contacts cluster before hard conversations and stressful weeks, not during crisis moments. What does this pattern represent?
choices: A sign that users are misusing the service and should be redirected to crisis resources.
The service's earned resume: what the market has actually decided to trust it with, regardless of the original design intent.
A data quality problem that requires a new tracking system before any conclusions can be drawn.
questions.explanation: Repeat hires in similar circumstances write the earned resume. The pre-crisis pattern is not a misuse finding. It is the market naming the job it has decided to trust the service with.

questions.prompt: A community college career program was designed for skill acquisition. Three cohorts show the same pattern: participants had already decided to change careers and used the credential to justify the decision to their families. What action best aligns the program with its earned resume?
choices: Add more skill modules to better match the original design intention.
Reframe outcomes, testimonials, and enrollment materials around the social proof job three cohorts have confirmed.
Survey the fourth cohort to see whether the pattern changes before making any design decisions.
questions.explanation: Three cohorts is a pattern, not a sample. The earned resume has been confirmed. The design question is whether to align the program with what the market has trusted, not whether to trust the pattern.

questions.prompt: Chris reviews two years of pet boarding intake surveys. The verbal handoff notes at pickup almost exclusively cover separation anxiety behavior, but the survey never asks about it. What does this reveal about the earned resume?
choices: The handoff notes are informal and should not be treated as evidence alongside structured survey data.
The survey should add more questions about feeding and exercise to better capture the range of client needs.
The facility has been hired to manage separation anxiety, but the intake process was measuring a different job entirely.
questions.explanation: The verbal notes capture what repeat clients actually care about at the handoff moment. Two years of that pattern is the earned resume. The survey was measuring around the job, not at it.

questions.prompt: Anke's photography studio was built around architecture and interior work. Repeat bookings come from event coordinators needing post-event documentation for grant accountability. The studio's website does not mention this work. What is the strategic risk of this gap?
choices: Clients who need documentary evidence work cannot find the service, and the studio's strongest competitive position has no voice in its marketing.
Naming the documentation work could dilute the architecture brand, making the studio look unfocused to clients who hire it for polished built-environment imagery.
The gap is a pricing risk: undocumented services may attract informal, low-quality inquiries, so the studio should raise rates before promoting the work.
questions.explanation: An earned resume that is invisible in marketing cannot attract the clients who most need it. The studio has built a competitive position it has not named. That silence is a cost, not a safety measure.

questions.prompt: Layla's tool library was built to reduce costs through shared equipment. The highest-repeat borrowers check out modest tools multiple times. The same homeowner rents a caulk gun three times in one year. What job has the library actually earned a resume for?
choices: Offering permission to attempt a task without committing to ownership if the attempt goes wrong.
Building community through shared physical resources and neighborhood connection.
Providing access to expensive tools that homeowners cannot afford to purchase.
questions.explanation: Renting a modest tool three times is not cost avoidance. It is repeated permission to try something uncertain. The earned resume is enabling the attempt, and that job has different design implications than cost sharing.

questions.prompt: A product team is planning an expansion into a new feature area. The proposal is adjacent to the existing product. Which question best tests whether the expansion respects the earned resume?
choices: Use competitive parity as the test, because leading competitors have already validated which adjacent features buyers expect in this market.
Use revenue potential as the test, because a large enough market can justify the build and trust can be earned after adoption begins.
Does the expansion extend a trust the market has already granted, or does it ask buyers to trust something the offering has not yet earned?
questions.explanation: The earned resume is a boundary as well as a foundation. Adjacency in product space does not guarantee adjacency in trust. The question is whether the market has given permission, not whether the team has capability.

questions.prompt: A team reviews five years of repeat purchases and finds two distinct patterns: some buyers return under high-stress deadlines and some buyers return for routine maintenance. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The product may have two distinct resumes that should be analyzed separately before claiming a unified identity.
The repeat use pattern is too varied to draw any conclusions about the earned resume.
The product has one resume that serves both types of buyers equally well.
questions.explanation: Repetition without consistent circumstances can hide two different resumes. A team that blends unlike jobs into one claimed identity will struggle to serve either job well and will claim a trust the market has not granted for the combined use case.

questions.prompt: Mikkel's cycling paths were built for commuters. Usage data shows twice as much weekend recreational use. A council liaison asks him to justify the original commuter investment. What is the most strategically honest response?
choices: Present the commuter data selectively to protect the original justification and revisit the recreational framing next budget cycle.
Argue that recreational use will eventually convert to commuter use as more riders build the habit.
Acknowledge the earned recreational resume and argue that the next phase of investment should be built around the job the market has actually confirmed.
questions.explanation: Defending a claimed identity against an earned one protects the original story at the cost of the real opportunity. The market has written the resume. The strongest next move is to build from it, not argue against it.

questions.prompt: A grant proposal for a crisis text line emphasizes crisis intervention outcomes. Usage data shows the strongest pattern is pre-crisis check-ins. Which framing best serves the organization's next funding cycle?
choices: Keep the crisis intervention framing because funders expect it and the pre-crisis work is harder to measure.
Describe the earned resume accurately, build measurement tools around the actual job, and seek funders whose priorities match pre-crisis maintenance.
Split the service into two programs to satisfy both the funder's expectations and the actual usage pattern.
questions.explanation: Funding for the wrong job creates pressure to perform on metrics that do not match actual impact. Describing the earned resume accurately and finding aligned funders is more sustainable than retrofitting the mission to meet mismatched expectations.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between a claimed identity and an earned resume?
reviewCards.back: A claimed identity is what the team says it offers. An earned resume is the pattern of jobs buyers have actually trusted it with through repeated hires. When those diverge, the earned resume is the stronger strategic signal.

reviewCards.front: Repeat use is high but the circumstances vary widely. What does that mean for the earned resume?
reviewCards.back: Repetition without consistent circumstances may hide two different resumes. Separate the patterns by situation and progress before claiming a unified identity. False unity leads to products that serve no job particularly well.

reviewCards.front: A team wants to expand into an adjacent feature area. How does the earned resume discipline that decision?
