reviewCards.back: Ask whether the expansion extends a trust the market has already granted or demands a new trust that has not been earned. Adjacency in product terms does not guarantee adjacency in buyer trust.

reviewCards.front: The earned resume does not match the stated mission. What is the first decision to make?
reviewCards.back: Decide whether to align the mission to the earned resume or invest in earning the resume the mission claims. Both are valid choices. The mistake is pretending the gap does not exist while building for the claimed identity.

reviewCards.front: A product is used heavily but the team cannot write one sentence naming the job. What does that signal?
reviewCards.back: The team has not yet read the pattern. Track repeat hires with circumstances attached. Who returned, under what pressure, for what progress. Without that specificity the resume is usage data, not earned trust.

implementationPlan.title: Reading the Pattern of Repeat Hires
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Read the pattern of repeat hires before writing the next product promise. The skill is to name who returned, under what pressure, and for what progress, then test whether the claimed identity matches the record the market has actually written.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a product proposal includes an expansion or repositioning, then write the earned resume first. Name the repeat hire pattern with circumstances attached before evaluating whether the new direction extends it.
If you keep returning to the same habit, tool, or routine, then name what job you are hiring it to do each time. The pattern you describe is your personal earned resume for that behavior.

If you are describing your skills to someone else, then check whether you are naming claimed capabilities or earned ones. The strongest answer is a pattern of situations where something you did produced a specific kind of progress.
If a recurring dynamic appears, then name what job that dynamic has earned a resume for before deciding whether to change it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, list five times someone has chosen you, your product, or your service more than once. Write one sentence for each naming the situation and the progress they were seeking. Look for the pattern that repeats.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, compare your stated value proposition to the actual pattern of repeat use. Write both in one sentence and identify where they match, where they diverge, and which one a new user would recognize when they first arrive.

memorableLines.text: The market has trusted the service with something specific and repeatable. That pattern is the most honest description of what the offering actually does well.
memorableLines.why: It frames the earned resume as an honest record, not a positioning choice.

memorableLines.text: The claimed identity reflects the team's original intention. The earned resume reflects what buyers have actually decided to rely on.
memorableLines.why: It names the gap cleanly and explains why the earned resume is the stronger strategic signal.

memorableLines.text: An offering earns its identity the same way a professional earns theirs: through repeated proof under pressure.
memorableLines.why: It makes the resume metaphor concrete and connects identity to demonstrated performance, not assertion.

chapters.title: Integrating Around a Job
chapters.hook: Grace's subscriber doesn't want Wednesday news on Friday. Both teams are hitting their numbers.
chapters.counterintuition: When every department meets its own target, the buyer's job can still break at the boundary between them. Despite appearances, local optimization is not coordination, and coordination is not integration.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name one internal decision from last month that improved one function's metric. Write a sentence on whether it made the buyer's progress easier or harder. If you cannot answer, no one was governing the tradeoff.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Integration around the job means one person or process governs the tradeoffs between functions so that each local win is tested against whether the buyer's full progress is protected.

breakdown.fastRead:
Grace's print and digital teams both hit their numbers this quarter. A subscriber calls to complain: the Wednesday property section she reads online is two weeks old by the time it posts. Both teams optimized their piece. Nobody governed the moment the subscriber hired the paper for: property news while it still matters.

This is the integration problem. When every department succeeds on its own metric, the buyer can still fail to get the job done. The job has to become the reference point across all the pieces, not just inside each one. Without a governing job, local wins add up to a buyer's loss.
breakdown.deepRead:
Coordination means people talk. Integration means someone governs tradeoffs by asking whether each local decision helps or hurts the buyer's full progress. Those are not the same thing.

At 7:38 a.m., Antoine's dispatch algorithm logs an 18 percent gain in delivery volume per courier-hour. Customer satisfaction scores fell the same week. The system optimized what the operations team measured. The clients hired the service to deliver time-sensitive documents with signature confirmation before 10 a.m. Two metrics. Two jobs. The algorithm served one and damaged the other because nobody was governing which job should win when they conflicted.

The allergy table in Giuliana's school cafeteria is clean, stocked, and certified. Safety protocols pass every inspection. A parent writes to say her son eats alone every day because none of his friends will sit there. Food services owned the safety job. The school's social environment job, belonging and learning together, was never coordinated into the same system of accountability. Two functions, each succeeding, with a gap between them that no one owned.

Integration requires naming the primary job the whole offering is hired for, then building a single accountability that crosses departmental lines. The job does not ask departments to stop having metrics. It asks that every metric be answerable to whether it helps or hurts the buyer's full progress. That is harder than a meeting. It requires someone to say, when your local win creates a gap in the buyer's path, your local win loses.

Local optimization is not coordination, and coordination is not integration.
breakdown.fullRead:
What happens when everyone does their job well? In most organizations, the answer is assumed to be obvious: the whole works. But the whole only works if the pieces were designed around the same reference point. When each piece was designed around its own metric, doing your job well can actively damage what the buyer hired.

This is the integration gap. It is not caused by failure. It is caused by partial optimization. The print team runs a P&L. The digital team runs a P&L. Both are rewarded for their own numbers. Nobody is rewarded for the moment the subscriber hired the newspaper to deliver: property news while it is still current, available in the format she chooses, on the day it matters. That moment lives in the gap between the two departments, and gaps are not managed by accident.

Jack is holding two documents at once: the plumber's as-built and the homeowner's tile pattern. The drain placement is correct per the plumber's scope. It is wrong for the tile layout the homeowner chose. Both contractors finished on time. Both delivered what they were hired for by their respective contracts. Nobody held the whole job: a functional, beautiful bathroom by move-in day. The homeowner is now absorbing the cost of coordinating two people who each did their work correctly. The integration gap is real, measurable, and it lives at the handoff.

Think about the last time a project went sideways even though each team delivered on time. Did anyone ask whether the handoffs between teams preserved the progress the buyer was trying to make? In most cases, the answer is no. The handoff is managed as a transfer of task, not a test of whether the buyer's job is still intact on the other side.

Hanna's transit agencies completed a genuine technical integration: three separate payment systems now speak to each other. It was expensive, it was slow, and it was celebrated internally. Six months later, cross-agency ridership in the overlap zone is flat. Exit surveys show riders still buying two day-passes because neither app shows combined journey time. The payment integration served the agencies' internal accounting job. It did not serve the rider's job: plan and execute an efficient multi-modal trip from one screen. The agencies coordinated. They did not integrate around the right job.

Hadiya's IT team completed every onboarding task within SLA. Hardware provisioned. Accounts created. Licenses assigned. Forty percent of new hires in the week-two survey still could not access the project management tool before their first team meeting. The access required a manager approval that IT does not own. The job (productive in team by week one) broke at the IT-to-manager boundary, not inside IT's scope. IT succeeded. The job failed. The boundary was unmanaged because the job was never the governing reference point across both functions.

Integration is a governance question, not just a coordination question. Governance means someone has authority to say: when your local optimization creates a gap in the buyer's progress, your optimization must change. Coordination without governance produces polite agreements that unravel at the first metric conflict.

The practical test: name the job the buyer hired, then trace the path to completed progress. Mark every handoff. At each handoff, ask whether someone is accountable for the job surviving the transfer. If the answer is no one, the job is unprotected at that boundary, and every local win on either side is provisional.

examples.title: Grace names the job the internal division is fracturing

planSpec.domain: regional newspaper (print and digital split P&L)
planSpec.stakes: two teams hit their numbers while the subscriber job breaks
planSpec.requiredBeat: both teams hitting their numbers while the subscriber job breaks at the boundary

examples.scenario: "Both teams are hitting their numbers," the publisher says, leaning back in the chair. Grace sets the subscriber complaint on the conference table. "Your Wednesday property section is two weeks old by the time I get the digital version." Print runs its own P&L. Digital runs its own. Neither is wrong on paper. Grace faces a choice: praise the quarterly results or name the job that the internal division is fracturing. The property editor is waiting on the phone for the verdict.
examples.whatToDo: Name the subscriber's job before discussing team metrics: timely property news in the format she chose. Map which boundary between print and digital caused the delay and assign a governing owner there.
examples.whyItMatters: Split P&Ls reward local performance and leave the boundary between them unmanaged. The job cannot survive a boundary no one owns.

examples.title: Antoine sees two metrics pointing at two different jobs

planSpec.stakes: volume optimization damages time-sensitive delivery job
planSpec.requiredBeat: efficiency gain and satisfaction drop reveal two metrics serving two different jobs

examples.scenario: At 7:38 a.m., Antoine reviews the dispatch dashboard. Efficiency per courier-hour is up 18 percent. He predicts a strong week. The client satisfaction report arrives at noon: scores fell. The algorithm routed for volume. The client's job is time-sensitive document delivery with signature confirmation before 10 a.m. The reveal is quiet and specific. Antoine must decide whether to attribute the gap to algorithm scope or to reconfigure what the dispatch system is being asked to optimize.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the two metrics by the job each serves. Ask which job the client hired the service to do, then make that job the constraint the algorithm must satisfy before optimizing anything else.
examples.whyItMatters: Two metrics measuring two different jobs will always conflict. The job that pays the client's contract should govern, not the one that is easier to track.

examples.title: Giuliana finds the allergy table clean and her student eating alone

planSpec.stakes: safety job and belonging job never coordinated
planSpec.requiredBeat: safety protocols pass while the belonging job breaks at the organizational boundary

examples.scenario: The allergy table smells of sanitizer and fresh fruit, every item labeled, every surface certified. Giuliana checks the safety log. Everything passes. A parent's note is clipped to the folder above the log: "My son eats alone every day because none of his friends will sit at the allergy table." Food services optimized for safety. The school's social environment, belonging and learning together, was never coordinated into the same accountability structure. Two jobs, two departments, no one governing the gap. Giuliana must decide whether to flag the coordination gap to the principal or absorb it as a food services redesign problem.
examples.whatToDo: Name both jobs explicitly: physical safety and social belonging. Assign someone to govern the boundary between food services and student life, with authority to require changes when one job breaks the other.
examples.whyItMatters: Two functions can each succeed on their own terms while a student pays the cost of the unmanaged gap between them. Integration requires the boundary to be owned.

examples.title: Jack holds the as-built and the tile pattern at the same time

planSpec.domain: home renovation contractor handoff (plumber to tile subcontractor)
planSpec.stakes: both contractors succeeded; nobody held the whole job
planSpec.requiredBeat: technically correct drain placement is wrong for the tile pattern; nobody held the whole bathroom job

examples.scenario: You are holding the plumber's as-built in one hand and the homeowner's tile pattern in the other. The drain is placed exactly where the spec said to put it. The tile pattern the homeowner chose requires a centered drain. Both contractors delivered their scopes on time and on budget. Neither was wrong on paper. You are about to decide whether to absorb the coordination cost now, before the tile goes down, or let the handoff complete and send the problem forward. The homeowner moves in on Friday.
examples.whatToDo: Stop the handoff before the tile goes down. Name the whole job: a functional, beautiful bathroom by move-in day. Assign that job as the governing reference for the scope conflict. The coordination cost now is cheaper than a floor tear-out.
examples.whyItMatters: Correct individual scopes do not guarantee the whole job survives the handoff. Someone has to hold the full job across contractors, or the buyer pays for the gap.

examples.title: Hanna reads flat ridership after the payment integration celebrated

planSpec.stakes: agencies integrated the wrong job and left the rider job unserved
planSpec.requiredBeat: payment integration served internal accounting; rider job of planning a multi-modal trip remained broken

examples.scenario: Hanna pulls the six-month ridership report and sets it beside the launch press release. The three-agency payment integration was technically successful. Cross-agency ridership in the overlap zone is flat. Exit surveys are plain: riders still buy two day-passes because neither app shows combined journey time. Payment integration served the agencies' accounting job. The rider's job, plan and execute an efficient multi-modal trip, was never integrated around.
examples.whatToDo: Restate the rider's job and test every integration decision against it. Combined journey time visibility is not a feature request; it is the integration the agencies did not build because they governed by their own accounting job.
examples.whyItMatters: Technical integration between systems can miss the buyer's job entirely if the governing question is internal efficiency instead of the rider's full progress.

examples.title: Hadiya traces the gap to the IT-to-manager boundary

planSpec.domain: corporate IT onboarding for new employees
planSpec.stakes: IT completed its scope; the job broke at the boundary IT does not own
planSpec.requiredBeat: IT completed within SLA; job broke at IT-to-manager boundary IT does not own

examples.scenario: Hadiya reviews the week-two onboarding survey. IT completed every task within SLA: hardware, accounts, licenses, access to company drives. Forty percent of new employees still could not access the project management tool before their first team meeting. The tool requires a manager approval step. IT does not own that step. The job, productive in team by week one, broke at the boundary between IT and the hiring manager, not inside IT's scope. IT's SLA was met. The job was not. Hadiya must decide whether to close the ticket as complete or reopen the process to include the manager approval step in the onboarding definition.
examples.whatToDo: Map the onboarding path to the job, not to departmental handoffs. Assign a single owner who is accountable for the job surviving every transfer, including the IT-to-manager step IT cannot control alone.
examples.whyItMatters: SLA completion inside one department does not protect a job that crosses multiple departments. The job needs a governing owner at every boundary, not just a checklist inside each scope.

questions.prompt: A print team and a digital team both hit their quarterly revenue targets. A subscriber complains that the digital property section is two weeks out of date. What does this situation most clearly illustrate?
choices: Local optimization by each team can break the buyer's job at the boundary between departments.
The subscriber is comparing the product against a competitor with faster publishing cycles.
Quarterly revenue is the correct signal for whether a buyer's job is being served.
questions.explanation: Both teams succeeded on their own metrics while the subscriber's job, timely property news, broke at the boundary between them. Meeting internal targets does not guarantee the buyer's progress is protected.

questions.prompt: A dispatch algorithm increases delivery volume per courier-hour by 18 percent. Client satisfaction scores fall the same week. Which question should the operations manager ask first?
choices: Which courier had the most complaints this week?
Which job was the algorithm governing, and is that the job the client hired the service to do?
Is the 18 percent gain large enough to offset the satisfaction drop in the next client contract review?
questions.explanation: Two metrics serving two different jobs will always conflict. The question is which job the client hired for, and whether the optimization served that job or a different internal one.

questions.prompt: A school's allergy accommodations pass every safety inspection. A parent reports her child eats alone daily because friends will not sit at the allergy table. Which diagnosis is most accurate?
choices: Food services and the student life function each succeeded on their own terms while the boundary between them went unmanaged.
The safety protocols are insufficient and need to be revised to include social accommodations.
Parents are setting expectations that go beyond what a school is hired to provide.
questions.explanation: Safety and belonging are two separate jobs, each owned by a different function. Neither failed within its own scope. The integration gap is the unmanaged boundary between them.

questions.prompt: A plumber places a drain correctly per spec. A tile subcontractor arrives and finds the drain is in the wrong position for the tile pattern the homeowner chose. Both contractors finished on time. What is the root cause of the problem?
choices: The tile subcontractor should have reviewed the plumber's as-built before the job started.
No one held the whole job across contractors, so a technically correct local scope created a defect in the buyer's full progress.
The homeowner made a tile pattern choice that was incompatible with standard drain placement.
questions.explanation: Each contractor succeeded inside their own scope. The integration gap is the absence of anyone governing the full job across the handoff between them.

questions.prompt: Three transit agencies integrate their payment systems. Six months later, cross-agency ridership is flat. Exit surveys show riders still buy two separate day-passes. What should the postmortem conclude?
choices: The payment integration was not technically complete and needs another phase.
Rider behavior is slow to change and the results should be measured over a longer period.
The integration served the agencies' internal accounting job rather than the rider's job of planning a multi-modal trip.
questions.explanation: Technical success between systems can miss the buyer's job entirely when the governing question is internal efficiency over the rider's full progress. The right job was never used as the integration target.

questions.prompt: IT completes onboarding within SLA. Forty percent of new employees cannot access the project management tool before their first team meeting because it requires a manager approval step IT does not own. What should the response be?
choices: Assign a governing owner for the onboarding job who is accountable across the IT-to-manager boundary, not just within IT's scope.
Revise the SLA to include manager approval and hold IT accountable for completion, since the current measurement boundary omits the failure point.
Automate manager approval so the handoff disappears, because removing manual action would prevent the access gap without changing ownership.
questions.explanation: The job broke at a boundary IT does not own. Adding SLA measures to IT for steps IT cannot control does not fix the integration gap. The fix is governance across the boundary.

questions.prompt: A manager says her team has weekly cross-functional meetings where all departments are represented. Buyers still report that their job breaks at handoffs. What does this situation reveal about the difference between coordination and integration?
choices: The meetings lack sufficient authority: departments are present but cannot make decisions in the room, so elevating attendees would make handoffs improve.
Coordination means people talk; integration means someone governs tradeoffs by testing whether the buyer's job survives each handoff.
The buyer reports are lagging while the meetings build familiarity, and handoffs should improve as teams better understand each other's constraints.
questions.explanation: Coordination and integration are different. Coordination creates shared information. Integration requires a governing authority that can require local changes when they damage the buyer's full progress.

questions.prompt: A team is proposing a new efficiency initiative that will reduce costs in one department by 12 percent. Before approving it, what is the integration test?
choices: Whether the 12 percent saving is large enough to offset any buyer dissatisfaction.
Whether the savings can be shared across departments to avoid internal resentment.
Whether the local efficiency gain helps or hurts the buyer's full progress across all handoffs.
questions.explanation: The integration test asks whether the local win serves or damages the buyer's job across the full path, not whether the saving is large enough to justify a tradeoff.

questions.prompt: Every department in a product organization reports that its metrics are green this quarter. The CEO wants to know whether this means the buyer's job is being protected. What analysis distinguishes local success from integration success?
choices: All-green departmental metrics are enough evidence that the organization is healthy, so the CEO should look for the one local metric that is not yet visible.
Compare customer satisfaction trends with the green metrics, because rising NPS would show the job is protected while divergence would identify the weak handoff.
Trace the buyer's path from first contact to completed progress, and test whether someone is accountable for the job surviving every handoff between departments.
questions.explanation: Green internal metrics do not guarantee the buyer's job is protected. Integration success requires a path analysis that checks whether the job survives each boundary, not just whether each department reported a good quarter.

reviewCards.front: Every department hit its target. A buyer still failed. What is the first question?
reviewCards.back: Ask where the buyer's progress broke. The failure is almost always at a boundary between functions, not inside any single department's scope. Identify which handoff was unmanaged.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between coordination and integration?
reviewCards.back: Coordination means people share information across functions. Integration means someone governs tradeoffs by testing whether the buyer's job survives every handoff. Only one of these protects the job when departments conflict.

reviewCards.front: Two departments each succeed on their own metrics. The buyer's job breaks. Where do you assign governance?
reviewCards.back: Assign governance at the boundary between the two departments, not inside either one. The governing owner needs authority to require changes from both functions when the buyer's full progress is at risk.

reviewCards.front: A technical integration between systems is technically complete. Buyers are not using it. What does the postmortem ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask which job the integration was built to serve. If it served an internal accounting or operational goal, not the buyer's progress, technical completeness is irrelevant to adoption.

reviewCards.front: What is the practical integration test before approving a local efficiency initiative?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the efficiency gain helps or hurts the buyer's full progress across all handoffs. A local win that creates a gap in the buyer's path is not an improvement to the offering, regardless of the departmental savings.

implementationPlan.title: Governing the Job Across Departmental Boundaries
implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is governing the job across departmental boundaries, not just inside each function. Trace the buyer's full path, mark every handoff, and assign accountability for the job surviving each transfer.

ifThenPlans.plan: If every department reports a win and a buyer still complains, then map the handoffs between functions and find the boundary where no one is governing the buyer's progress.
If a health routine is technically correct at each step but not producing progress, then trace which handoff between steps is unmanaged and assign yourself the governing responsibility there.
If a project involves multiple people each doing their part, then name the whole job in writing and check that someone is accountable for it at every transfer point.

If a shared task keeps breaking despite everyone doing their assigned part, then hold a meeting where the job is named first and each person's role is evaluated by whether it helps the whole job, not just their portion.

chapters.title: Keeping Your Eye on the Job
chapters.hook: Chidi's contract pays more. His regulars hired the truck for Tuesday, not lunch.
chapters.counterintuition: A change that passes every internal review can still abandon the buyer's job. Even though it looks locally harmless, the job-first test is not applied automatically; it has to be a required step before approval.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name a change approved last month without asking the job question. Write what it improved internally. Then write whether it made the buyer's progress more or less protected. If both answers are positive, check your work.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Apply the job-first test to every proposed change before approving: ask not whether it improves internally, but whether it makes the buyer's progress clearer, safer, faster, or more complete.

breakdown.fastRead:
Chidi has a corporate catering contract that would take his food truck off his regular corner three days a week. The revenue model says yes. His regular customers are not hiring lunch. They are hiring the steady midweek punctuation, the truck being there on Tuesday when the week gets hard. The contract is not a growth win. It is a job-abandonment decision wearing the disguise of a revenue gain.

This is what drift looks like from the inside: a change that improves something real, passes every obvious review, and still abandons the job buyers hired. Keeping focus on the job means applying the job-first test before approving the change, not after.
breakdown.deepRead:
The job-first test asks one question about any proposed change: does this make the buyer's desired progress more or less protected? It is not the same as asking whether the change is good for the business. Internal improvements, cost reductions, and revenue expansions can all pass internal review while failing the job-first test.

Olivier faces this in a bootcamp curriculum review. An alumni advisory board member is direct: "The ML module takes six weeks from fundamentals. That's six weeks of job-ready time spent on terminology that impresses hiring managers who don't actually hire bootcamp grads for ML." The job buyers hired is ready to contribute to a working codebase in week one. The drift is optimizing for what sounds impressive instead of testing every module against the employment job. Nobody made a bad decision in isolation. Each module addition was defensible. The job-first test was never required as a gate.

Drift is hardest to see when the change is genuinely positive in one dimension. A biweekly ordering cycle that cuts logistics costs by 14 percent is a real improvement. A weekly rhythm that lets members know what will be on the shelf Sunday is also real. When those two conflict, the job-first test asks which one the buyer hired. If 38 percent of survey comments reference shelf predictability, the buyer may have hired the weekly rhythm, not the biweekly savings. The test has to be applied before the decision is framed as purely operational.

The job-first test requires someone to ask the question, have authority to require a job-framed answer, and be willing to block approvals when the answer is absent or evasive. That is organizational discipline, not individual insight.

The test has to happen before approval, not in the postmortem.
breakdown.fullRead:
Most organizations apply tests at the end of a decision process. Did we hit budget? Did the feature ship on time? Did client satisfaction hold? These are reasonable measures, but they are all internal. The job-first test is different because it is applied before the decision is finalized, and it measures the change against the buyer's progress rather than the company's operations. The job-first test is not applied automatically; it has to be a required step before approval, especially when the change looks locally harmless.

Laura's architecture firm has a new virtual walkthrough tool. Feedback cycles shortened. The visualization improved. The hospital facilities director said in a side conversation: "The walkthroughs are beautiful. But I don't know what I'm approving anymore." The tool improved a real thing. It also blurred the approval-readiness job. The client's job is not to see a beautiful building. The client's job is to reach a point where they know what they are signing off on. Laura is weighing whether to deploy before applying the job-first test, and the side conversation is the only signal that something may be off.

Here is a useful provocation: think about the last change your own team made that was internally celebrated. Did anyone ask whether it made the buyer's job easier to complete, or just whether it improved a metric you were already measuring? In most teams, the internal metric review happened and the job question was not required. That asymmetry is how drift accumulates.

Tomas's non-emergency routing change passed every available internal test. Response times stayed within acceptable range. Overtime costs dropped. The protocol looked like a straightforward operational improvement. Three months later, a kitchen fire escalated because a non-duty responder hit a roster gap the protocol created. The job-first test was not applied before approval: does this make reliable emergency response more or less protected? The answer might have been visible in scenario modeling if the question had been required. It was not required, so it was not asked.

Nina is holding the recommendation for the cooperative grocery store. Biweekly ordering cuts logistics costs by 14 percent. Thirty-eight percent of member survey comments reference knowing what will be on the shelf Sunday. The weekly rhythm creates a predictability contract. Biweekly breaks that job even as it improves the operational one. The job-first test is available before the recommendation goes forward. Whether it gets applied is a question of organizational discipline, not data availability.

The discipline is a simple requirement: before any proposed change is approved, someone must state the buyer's job in one sentence and answer whether the change makes that job more or less protected. If the answer is uncertain, the approval is deferred until the uncertainty is resolved. This is not a guarantee of perfect decisions. It is a guarantee that the buyer's job is a required input to every decision, not an afterthought when the damage is already done.

The module scores well on student surveys. Employers in the advisory group rated the graduates as technically current. The job buyers hired: ready to contribute to a working codebase in week one. Olivier is about to respond to the feedback.

examples.whyItMatters: Curriculum additions that impress the wrong audience are a form of job drift. The test is not whether the content is valuable in the abstract but whether it serves the job the buyer hired.

planSpec.requiredBeat: non-emergency routing reduces overtime; three months later a fire escalates through a roster gap the protocol created

He predicts a clean operational win. Three months later, a kitchen fire escalates. A non-duty responder hit a roster gap the routing protocol created. The postmortem is not about the fire. It is about the question that was not required before approval: does this change make reliable emergency response more or less protected? planSpec.requiredBeat: library scores positively internally; consultants use it for presentations; advisory judgment job went underserved

He pulls the usage logs: the library is used most heavily in the 48 hours before client presentations. It is not showing up in the project work phases where recommendations are formed. The firm is hired to give clients advice they cannot generate internally. The library is being used to prepare how advice looks, not to improve what the advice is.
examples.whatToDo: Restate the firm's job before reviewing the library's design. For each feature, ask: does this help consultants form better recommendations or just present them more confidently? Redirect toward the former.
examples.whyItMatters: A tool that earns high internal scores while serving a secondary job is a drift signal, not a success signal. The job-first test applied after deployment is better than never, but it is costlier than applying it before launch.

examples.title: Nina faces the shelf-predictability contract before the recommendation goes forward

planSpec.requiredBeat: biweekly ordering improves logistics cost; 38 percent of member comments reference shelf predictability; Nina faces the recommendation decision

examples.scenario: You are Nina, preparing the recommendation for the cooperative's ordering cycle review. The biweekly shift cuts logistics costs by 14 percent. The member survey is open on your screen: 38 percent of comments reference knowing what will be on the shelf this Sunday. The weekly rhythm is not just a preference; it is the predictability contract members hired the cooperative for. Biweekly breaks that job even as it improves the operational one. Your recommendation is due before the board meeting closes. You must choose whether to recommend the biweekly shift or hold the weekly rhythm.
examples.whatToDo: Apply the job-first test before the recommendation: state the member's job (predictable shelf access), then evaluate whether the logistics saving is worth disrupting the contract members hired the cooperative for.
examples.whyItMatters: A logistics improvement that disrupts a job members hired for is not a straightforward operational win. The job-first test makes the tradeoff visible before it is approved, not after members start shopping elsewhere.

examples.title: Chidi frames the catering contract as a job-abandonment question

planSpec.stakes: catering revenue growth is actually a job-abandonment decision
planSpec.requiredBeat: regular customers hired predictable midweek presence, not lunch; the contract is a job-abandonment decision

examples.scenario: When did you last ask what your regulars actually hired you for? Chidi is holding a corporate catering contract that would take the truck off his regular corner three days a week. The revenue model says yes without hesitation. The regulars who appear at noon on Tuesday are not hiring lunch. They are hiring the predictable midweek punctuation, the truck being there when the week gets hard. The catering contract is a job-abandonment decision wearing the disguise of a revenue gain. Chidi must decide whether to take the contract or hold his corner.
examples.whatToDo: Apply the job-first test before signing: state the job regulars hired the truck for. If three days away per week makes that job less reliably delivered, name the contract as a tradeoff and decide it deliberately.
examples.whyItMatters: Revenue growth that abandons the job buyers hired for is not growth of the business they hired. The job-first test makes the abandonment decision visible so it can be made intentionally.

questions.prompt: A software tool improves feedback cycle speed for an architecture client. A facilities director says in a side conversation that he no longer knows what he is approving. What does this reveal about the proposed change?
choices: The feedback cycle improvement was not large enough to matter to the client.
The client's preference for slower tools should be accommodated as a service exception.
The change improved one internal metric while weakening the buyer's approval-readiness job.
questions.explanation: Faster feedback cycles and clearer approval readiness can point in different directions. The side conversation is the signal that the job-first test was not applied before the tool was deployed.

questions.prompt: A coding bootcamp's ML module earns strong student survey scores but uses six weeks of time that advisors say should be spent on job-ready fundamentals. What should the program director do before the next curriculum cycle?
choices: Apply the job-first test to every module: ask whether each one makes graduates more or less ready to contribute to a working codebase in week one.
Weight the survey scores heavily because satisfaction predicts completion and referrals, and lowering scores may cost more than reclaiming the six weeks.
Ask hiring managers to rank in-demand topics and compare that list to the curriculum, treating labor-market demand as the test of relevance.
questions.explanation: Strong internal survey scores do not confirm the module serves the employment job. The job-first test requires asking whether the content serves the buyer's progress, not whether students find it interesting.

questions.prompt: A volunteer fire department changes non-emergency routing to reduce overtime. Response times stay within range. Three months later, a fire escalates because of a roster gap the protocol created. What was missing from the approval process?
choices: A financial review of the overtime savings against the long-term cost of emergency escalation.
A required job-first test asking whether the protocol change made reliable emergency response more or less protected.
A committee vote on whether the overtime savings were worth the operational risk.
questions.explanation: The approval process had operational and financial tests but not the job-first test. Requiring that test before approval would have forced the question of emergency reliability into the decision.

questions.prompt: A consulting firm's case library earns high internal scores. Usage logs show it is used primarily before presentations, not during recommendation development. Client satisfaction is flat. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
choices: Client satisfaction is a lagging indicator and will improve as consultants use the library more.
The library was built for the consultant's presentation job instead of the advisory judgment job the firm is hired to deliver.
The library needs more content before it can affect recommendation quality.
questions.explanation: High internal scores and frequent use do not confirm the tool serves the buyer's job. The usage pattern reveals which job the tool actually serves, and it is not the one that produces client satisfaction.

questions.prompt: A cooperative grocery store can shift to biweekly ordering and cut logistics costs by 14 percent. Thirty-eight percent of member comments reference knowing what will be on the shelf each Sunday. Before approving the change, what does the job-first test require?
choices: Calculate whether the 14 percent saving is large enough to compensate dissatisfied members.
Survey members on whether they prefer cost savings or shelf predictability.
State the member's job explicitly and answer whether biweekly ordering makes that job more or less protected.
questions.explanation: The job-first test requires naming the job before evaluating the change. A savings calculation and a preference survey both skip the step of defining what buyers hired the cooperative to deliver.

questions.prompt: A food truck operator is offered a corporate catering contract that would take the truck off its regular corner three days a week. The revenue is meaningful. What does the job-first test ask before the contract is signed?
choices: Whether the catering revenue can be reinvested in marketing to attract new regular customers.
Whether the contract requires the truck to leave the corner on the days regulars show up most.
Whether three days away per week makes the predictable midweek presence job more or less reliably delivered for regular customers.
questions.explanation: The job regulars hired for is not lunch; it is a predictable presence at a specific time. The job-first test asks whether the contract change protects or abandons that job, not whether the revenue is attractive.

questions.prompt: A team says its job is still the priority and that the new process change aligns with it. A manager wants to test whether this is true. What distinguishes a tested claim from a stated one?
choices: The team can show that the change, when traced through the buyer's path, makes their desired progress clearer or more complete.
Use stakeholder alignment as the test: if leadership and partner functions agree the change supports the job, disagreement would have surfaced during review.
Use post-deployment metrics as the test, because improved performance after launch gives cleaner evidence than tracing buyer progress before release.
questions.explanation: Stating that the job is a priority is not the same as testing whether a specific change serves it. The test requires tracing the change through the buyer's progress, not through the internal strategy document.

questions.prompt: A team discovers in a postmortem that a change approved six months ago was actually a job-abandonment decision. They want to prevent this in the future. Which process change is most likely to help?
choices: Require that every proposed change include a statement of the buyer's job and an answer to whether the change makes that job more or less protected, before approval.
Require a 60-day postmortem after each major launch with a standing question about job protection, creating learning without slowing approvals.
Add a jobs-focused reviewer to the approval chain, so a specialist flags abandonment risk instead of asking every team to write the analysis.
questions.explanation: A postmortem finds the problem after the damage is done. Requiring the job-first test before approval prevents the decision from being made without the buyer's job as a required input.

questions.prompt: An operations director argues that a new efficiency initiative is not a job question because it only affects internal processes. What is the strongest counterargument?
choices: Many internal processes affect how buyers experience progress, so a process change can still be a job question even when the work is not customer-facing.
The efficiency initiative may pass every internal test while changing how buyers experience the path to their desired progress.
Internal process changes are exempt from the job-first test if they do not touch customer-facing features.
questions.explanation: The job-first test applies to any change that affects the buyer's path, including internal processes that alter handoffs, timing, or quality. Whether a change is internal does not determine whether it affects the buyer's job.

reviewCards.front: A change passed every internal review. How do you apply the job-first test?
reviewCards.back: State the buyer's job in one sentence and ask whether the change makes that job clearer, safer, faster, or more complete. Internal approval does not answer this question.

reviewCards.front: A tool improves something real and earns positive internal scores. What signal suggests drift?
reviewCards.back: Check how buyers are using it and whether client outcomes improved. High internal scores combined with flat or declining buyer outcomes indicate the tool serves an internal job, not the buyer's job.

reviewCards.front: What distinguishes stating that the job is a priority from testing it?
reviewCards.back: A stated priority appears in documents and presentations. A tested priority requires tracing each proposed change through the buyer's path and showing that the change makes their desired progress more protected, not just that it aligns with stated strategy.

reviewCards.front: A revenue opportunity conflicts with the buyer's job. What does the job-first test require?
reviewCards.back: Name the conflict explicitly before approving. The test does not prohibit taking the opportunity, but it requires the abandonment decision to be made intentionally, not by default, with the job clearly named as the cost.

reviewCards.front: Where in the decision process should the job-first test be applied?
reviewCards.back: Before approval, not in a postmortem. The test is most valuable when it is a required input to the decision, not a retrospective explanation of why something did not work after the change was already made.

implementationPlan.title: Applying the Job-First Test to Changes
implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is applying the job-first test as a required gate before approving any change, not as an optional reflection afterward. This requires naming the buyer's job in one sentence and testing the proposed change against it.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a proposed change is presented without a statement of the buyer's job, then require the proposer to add that statement and answer whether the change makes that job more or less protected before the review continues.
If a new health routine improvement looks appealing, then write the job the routine is hired for and ask whether the improvement makes that job easier to complete or just easier to report.
If a new opportunity would require dropping something regular customers or users rely on, then name the job they hired you for before calculating the revenue or efficiency gain.
If a change to a regular commitment seems harmless on paper, then ask the other person what they hired that commitment for before deciding the change is safe.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, take one change currently under consideration and apply the job-first test in writing: state the buyer's job in one sentence, describe what the change improves internally, and write a clear answer to whether the change makes the buyer's job more or less protected.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review one approved change from the past month and ask whether the job-first test was applied before approval. If it was not, write what the test would have asked and whether the answer would have changed the decision.

memorableLines.why: It names the disguise that makes drift hard to see and gives it a precise label.

memorableLines.text: The job-first test is not applied automatically; it has to be a required step before approval, especially when the change looks locally harmless.
memorableLines.why: It explains why good intentions are not sufficient and why the test must be structural.
